A 7-week-old, previously healthy full-term male infant presented with a 4-week history of a worsening, widespread, papulopustulovesicular eruption, which began as scattered papulovesicles over the chest. No excoriations were visible. The sitter had provided domestic care for the infant since birth until leaving that position 3 weeks earlier.On examination, the infant was afebrile with normal vital signs. The parents denied any personal or family history of rash. The mother had a benign prenatal course during pregnancy. Since the rash developed, the infant had been fussy with increasing restlessness at night. The infant was born to a 31-year-old mother by normal vaginal delivery. On further questioning, the parents reported that the infant had had contact with a babysitter who reported pruritus, especially at night. A Tzanck smear showed no multinucleated giant cells in the pustular contents. Cultures of the pustular contents yielded no bacterial or fungal growth. A Gram stain and potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of the pustular contents showed no bacterial or fungal elements. Multiple disseminated, edematous, pin-sized, papulopustulovesicles and 5- to 10-mm coalescing, crusted nodules were found all over the body; some with oval to elongated, serpiginous or J-shaped burrows (Figure 1).

He lived in rural China and had close contact with dogs, cattle, and sheep. A 62-year-old woman is brought to a physician by her husband for fluctuating changes in behavior and hallucinations over the past 2 years. He also reported a vague feeling of perplexity and derealization. He reported that he no longer enjoyed his former interests and could not relate to people at college or to friends, but there were no clear signs of depressive disorders. The mother denies that anyone in the house smokes. The newborn had been sleeping regularly and feeding well. Figure A shows a photograph of one of the patient's eyes. The patient's physical exam is otherwise unrevealing. This morning, the newborn developed a thick yellow-white eye discharge. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated.

On physical exam, the patient has a flat affect with a facial grimace and sudden jerky movements of his upper extremities. A 46-year-old man presents with his wife to his primary care provider for depression and strange movements. His family history is unknown as he was adopted. His wife reports that her husband has not been himself for the last 2 months. His wife says that he is getting worse. The patient’s medical history is significant for hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril. He drinks a few glasses of wine per week and has never smoked. The patient met his mother once and never knew his father but was told he died in his 50s. Whereas he was previously outgoing and “the life of the party,” the patient is now irritable and withdrawn. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 141/87 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min. The patient cannot explain the recent changes to his mood and tearfully admits he fears there is something seriously wrong with him. He is a partner at an accounting firm, but his colleagues are threatening to fire him if he continues to perform poorly at work.

Her BMI is 32.4 kg/m^2. A transvaginal ultrasound is performed and demonstrates two intramural leiomyomas. She has a medical history of hypertension for which she takes hydrochlorothiazide. A 36-year-old woman, G1P1001, presents to her gynecologist for an annual visit. The patient’s mother had breast cancer at age 68, and her sister has endometriosis. A pelvic exam reveals a non-tender, 12-week-size uterus with an irregular contour. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 138/74 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 13/min. She states that she feels well and has no complaints.

A 47-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a headache. He suddenly developed a throbbing, bitemporal headache about 5 hours ago "out of nowhere." On physical exam, he appears to be in moderate distress and has pain with neck flexion. He has a history of migraine headaches, but he feels that this headache is significantly more painful than his typical migraines. He has no focal neurologic deficits. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 147/91 mmHg, pulse is 62/min, and respirations are 12/min. The patient denies any recent trauma to the head. His medical history is significant for migraines and hypertension. A head CT is performed and can be seen in Figure A. He also endorses nausea and he reports that he vomited once before arrival in the emergency department. He drinks 5-6 beers per week. He has a 20-pack-year smoking history and a history of cocaine use. The patient took his prescribed sumatriptan with no relief of his symptoms.

A 25-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with anxiety and fatigue. During this past week, he has been unable to properly study and prepare for final exams because he is exhausted. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 115/71 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. The patient states that he fears he will fail his courses if he does not come up with a solution. His neurological exam is within normal limits. Otherwise, the patient has no significant medical history and is not taking any medications. On physical exam, the patient is a tired and anxious appearing young man. He has been going to bed early but is unable to get a good night’s sleep. He admits to occasional cocaine and marijuana use.

A 27-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for exposure to toxic materials. The patient states that when he left for work this morning he was certain that he had closed the door to his pantry. The patient is certain that his neighbors have been tampering with his food and potentially poisoned him. The patient is outraged at this news and requests a competent doctor who is not colluding with his enemies. He further states that he knows they have been trying to break into his house and steal his things. It is for this reason that he is certain that they are trying to get their revenge upon him. He has tried multiple times to get them evicted from the building to no avail. Upon returning home, he saw that the door to his pantry was wide open. The physician performs a physical exam and tells the patient that he thinks there is nothing to be concerned about, but that he should call him or come into the office if he experiences any symptoms. He storms out of the office angrily, stating that he deserves the best in medical care. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 115/71 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min.

His medical history includes type 1 diabetes mellitus and an episode of herpes zoster on his right flank 1 year ago. The episodes start suddenly and feel like a stabbing, electrical pain over his left eye. He reports that he has headaches at night several times a week. A CT of the head and sinuses shows no acute abnormalities. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 112/69 mmHg, pulse is 61/min, and respirations are 14/min. His only home medication is insulin. He first developed these headaches over 1 year ago, but they started up again 3 weeks ago. He also reports tearing of the left eye during these episodes. On physical exam, his extraocular muscles are intact and his eyes are not injected. A 32-year-old man presents to his primary care provider for a headache. The headaches self-resolve over the course of 2-3 hours, but the patient complains that he is avoiding going to sleep for fear of waking up in pain.

The mass medially deviated the left optic nerve and conformed to the shape of the orbital globe with mild bony remodeling of the lateral orbital wall.T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging of the brain shows a 2.3-cm intraconal mass (black asterisk) molding to the left orbital globe with medial deviation of the optic nerve (blue asterisk). Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (Figure 1) showed a 2.3-cm intraconal mass inseparable from the left lateral rectus muscle. Both optic nerves appeared normal on retinal examination. Her medical history includes breast cancer, diagnosed in 2000 and treated with lumpectomy and radiotherapy. A mammogram, completed 4 months before her ophthalmology visit, was reported as stable. More recently, she noted that her left eye “drifts out at times.” She also reported drooping of the left upper eyelid and binocular, variable horizontal or vertical diplopia at distance. . She had slightly decreased color vision (8/10 Ishihara plates) of the left eye and there was no relative afferent pupillary defect. A woman in her 60s presented to the ophthalmology clinic with 10 months of blurred vision in her left eye. Confrontation visual fields were full. On presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS. External examination revealed mild left proptosis and severely limited adduction of the left eye. She also complained of itchy eyes but denied any pain or headaches.

Every few weeks she has an episode of a right-sided, throbbing headache. A 28-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider with a headache. On physical exam, the patient has no focal neurologic deficits. The patient denies any weakness, numbness, or tingling during these episodes. The episodes began several years ago and are accompanied by nausea and bright spots in her vision. A CT of the head is performed and shows no acute abnormalities. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 125/81 mmHg, pulse is 64/min, and respirations are 11/min. She works as a receptionist at a marketing company. Her home medications include levothyroxine, oral contraceptive pills, and topical trans-retinoin. She has 2 glasses of wine with dinner several nights a week and has never smoked. Her medical history is significant for acne, hypothyroidism, obesity, and endometriosis. The headache usually subsides if she lies still in a dark, quiet room for several hours.

His medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and a prior transient ischemic attack. He is difficult to arouse with a GCS of 7. His medications include atorvastatin and lisinopril. A head CT is performed and can be seen in Figure A. The patient initially denied medical treatment but his wife convinced him to be taken by ambulance to the emergency department for evaluation. The paramedics report that at the scene the patient had a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 15. When he woke up, he was mildly confused but able to ski down the rest of the mountain. In the emergency department, his temperature is 97.8°F (36.6°C), blood pressure is 141/84 mmHg, pulse is 71/min, and respirations are 16/min. During the ride, he became gradually more somnolent. He lost consciousness for about 30 seconds. A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a skiing accident. The patient lost control of his skis and collided with a tree.

Thick exudate is draining from an opening in the skin. Two months ago, the patient had a root canal on a left molar. On physical exam, there is a bluish hue to the skin on the lower left side of the patient’s face. A 3x4 cm non-tender mass can be palpated inferior to the angle of the left mandible. Over the past week, she has had increasing difficulty chewing her food and progressive pain in the left side of her jaw. The gram stain of the exudate can be seen in Figure A. She has never smoked and has 10-15 alcoholic drinks per week. A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with difficulty eating. This morning, she was unable to close her mouth for several minutes after taking a bite of her breakfast. Her temperature is 100.8°F (38.2°C), blood pressure is 133/74 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 14/min. Her medical history is significant for hyperlipidemia, mild intermittent asthma, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She works as an aide at a nursing home.

An MRI of the head is obtained and reveals cerebral edema. A lumbar puncture reveals an increased opening pressure with a normal glucose level. Fundoscopic exam reveals mild bilateral papilledema. The patient has had headaches in the past but this is the worst headache of her life. Her symptoms started yesterday and have been getting progressively worse. There has been a recent outbreak of measles at the patient’s school and the patient’s mother has been trying to give her daughter medicine to prevent her from getting sick. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 123/74 mmHg, pulse is 85/min, and respirations are 13/min. A 17-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a headache. . Her neurological exam is within normal limits. The patient states that the pain is mostly on the left side of her head. On exam, the patient is an obese girl who is clutching her head with the light in the room turned off. Her mother fears that her daughter may have caught measles.

A 45-year-old man with history of IV drug use presents to the outpatient clinic with a history of fever for 5 days. He also endorses sweats, headache behind the eyes, sore throat, muscle and joint pain, and a new rash seen in Figure A. ALP: 78 IU/L His temperature is 101.5°F (38.6°C), blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 14/min. Leukocyte count: 2,400/mm^3 His immunizations are up to date, although he missed the pre-departure travel medicine consult before his trip to Thailand. AST: 112 IU/L ALT: 69 IU/L Platelets: 92,000/mm^3 Mean corpuscular volume: 81 µm^3 Serum: Hematocrit: 40% Bilirubin: 0.9 mg/dL Hemoglobin: 13.4 g/dL He reports that he traveled to Africa last year and returned from a vacation to Thailand 10 days ago. Laboratory testing reveals the following:

He endorses a history of unprotected sex with multiple partners and intravenous drug use during a recent vacation to Mexico but has no other significant medical history. The scan also shows a large liver mass measuring 6 cm as seen in Figure A. A CT of the abdomen confirms appendicitis. He has significant acne on his face, chest, and back. He has had vague, mild discomfort in the right upper quadrant since the start of this wrestling season. Physical exam demonstrates pain on palpation of the right lower quadrant and mild pain in the right upper quadrant. He drinks socially and has never smoked. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 119/72 mmHg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 12/min. He also endorses loss of appetite and subjective fever. A 21-year-old man presents to the emergency room with right lower quadrant pain that started this afternoon at his wrestling match.

A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency room reporting sudden-onset abdominal and back pain that began 3 hours ago. Repeat blood pressure is 87/50 and pulse is 127. During evaluation, the patient becomes diaphoretic and pale and reports that he feels fatigued. He denies any diarrhea or hematochezia and says the pain is not affected by movement. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and depression. . Intravenous fluid boluses are administered. He currently takes amlodipine and atorvastatin and is compliant with his medications. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history, but he does not drink alcohol or use any illicit drugs. Physical exam is notable for diffuse abdominal tenderness without rigidity or guarding. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), his blood pressure is 110/64 mmHg, pulse is 97/min, and respirations are 15/min. He was eating dinner when he started feeling severe pain in his abdomen that made him lose his appetite.

She had unprotected sexual intercourse earlier that morning and requests emergency contraception. The patient asks for an emergency contraceptive pill and would prefer that her parents not be notified about her visit. She has no significant medical history. She has had regular menses since menarche, and her last menstrual period ended 8 days ago. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 114/71 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min. A physical exam is unremarkable. A 15-year-old girl presents to the clinic due to concern that she may be pregnant.

When he was lifting a heavy object, he suddenly felt pain in his lower back. He describes the pain as in his buttocks but states that at times it travels down his leg. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 131/82 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 14/min. The patient has a medical history of obesity, diabetes, depression, anxiety, diverticulosis, constipation, and a surgical repair of his anterior cruciate ligament. An exam of the cranial nerves is intact bilaterally. No clonus or Babinski sign is appreciated. His current medications include metformin, insulin, lisinopril, fluoxetine, and sodium docusate. He states that it feels electrical and burning in nature. A 69-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with hip and back pain. On physical exam, he is found to have an intact motor and sensory function in his lower extremities bilaterally. He states this weekend he had a barbecue.

A 25-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for trouble with focus and concentration. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min. His boss will have to yell at him to startle him back to work. Ever since the patient started working, he has had trouble focusing on his job. A physical exam is within normal limits. His boss often observes him "daydreaming" with a blank stare off into space. The patient states that he feels fatigued all the time and sometimes will suddenly fall asleep while operating equipment. He is unable to stay focused on any task. He has tried going to bed early for the past month but is unable to fall asleep until 2 hours prior to his alarm. He states that he lives at home with his parents his entire life and recently was able to get a job at a local factory. The patient fears that if this continues he will lose his job.

A woman in her 60s presented with a 3-month history of a progressive, asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on her chest and back. In 2014, she developed axillary lymphadenopathy on the right side and was found to have metastatic disease. At the time of her evaluation, the patient’s physical examination was remarkable for discrete erysipeloid plaques on her chest, back, and right shoulder (Figure 1A). She had a complex history of breast cancer on the left side that was first diagnosed in 1991 and was treated with lumpectomy, radiotherapy, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, and fluorouracil. Lesional skin biopsies were performed (Figure 1B).A, Clinical examination shows discrete erysipeloid plaques on the anterior chest. She subsequently underwent axillary lymph node dissection on the right side, followed by treatment with doxorubicin hydrochloride and cyclophosphamide. B, Histopathologic analysis (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×100). In 2001, she experienced local disease recurrence and underwent complete mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection on the left side and received adjuvant treatment with tamoxifen citrate and anastrozole. Her most recent mammogram and positron-emission tomography–computed tomography (PET/CT) showed no evidence of active disease. Serum chemistry profile, complete blood cell counts, and hepatic and renal function testing had normal results. . The lesions were warm and indurated but nontender to palpation.

The patient is sent for a right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrating an absence of stones, no pericholecystic fluid, a normal gallbladder contour and no abnormalities noted in the common bile duct. A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fluctuating right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Her current medications include metformin, glyburide, escitalopram, and psyllium husks. The patient has a medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, depression, anxiety, and irritable bowel syndrome. ALT: 110 U/L Bilirubin Alkaline phosphatase: 125 U/L Her lab values and clinical presentation remain unchanged 24 hours later. On exam, the patient is an obese woman with pain upon palpation of the right upper quadrant. HCO3-: 24 mEq/L Initial labs are are below: Direct: 1.8 mg/dL Total: 2.5 mg/dL Her temperature is 99.2°F (37.3°C), pulse of 95/min, blood pressure of 135/90 mmHg, respirations of 15/min with 98% oxygen saturation on room air. Na+: 140 mEq/L Amylase: 30 U/L The pain was initially a 4/10 in severity but has increased recently to a 6/10 prompting her to come in. AST: 100 U/L K+: 4.0 mEq/L Cl-: 100 mEq/L MRCP with secretin infusion is performed demonstrating patent biliary and pancreatic ductal systems.

The patient's treatment history is significant for failure to obtain symptom control with risperidone, haloperidol, and ziprasidone. He is currently homeless. The patient has a medical history of marijuana and IV drug use as well as multiple suicide attempts. Though he is no longer aggressive, he is seen making "armor" out of paper plates and plastic silverware to defend himself. A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department. The patient is transferred to the inpatient psychiatric unit and is continued on haloperidol throughout the next week. While in the ED, the patient is combative and refuses a physical exam. He was brought in by police for shouting on a subway. He is given IM haloperidol and diphenhydramine. The patient claims that little people were trying to kill him and he was acting within his rights to defend himself. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 115/71 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min.

The patient's teacher describes her as occasionally "daydreaming" for periods of time during where the patient does not respond or participate in school activities. Nothing has helped the patient change her behavior, including parent-teacher conferences or punishment. A 16-year-old girl who recently immigrated to the United States from Bolivia presents to her primary care physician with a chief complaint of inattentiveness in school. On physical exam, you note a young, healthy girl whose neurological exam is within normal limits. The patient has an unknown medical history and is currently not on any medications. The patient states she is not doing this intentionally. The patient has no other concerns. She is not sexually active and does not intend to become pregnant in the near future. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 112/74 mmHg, pulse is 63/min, and respirations are 11/min. The only other concern that the patient's mother has is that, upon awakening, she notices that sometimes the patient's arm will jerk back and forth.

Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 115/71 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. Creatinine: 1.7 mg/dL Na+: 137 mEq/L Based on the results of a doppler ultrasound of her swollen lower extremity, heparin is started. The patient has a medical history of obesity, diabetes, bipolar disorder, and tonic-clonic seizures. Ca2+: 5.7 mg/dL K+: 5.5 mEq/L Cl-: 100 mEq/L Glucose: 70 mg/dL. Physical exam reveals anasarca and asymmetric lower extremity swelling. Urea nitrogen: 22 mg/dL Her current medications include metformin, insulin, lisinopril, and valproic acid. The patient is then transferred to the general medicine floor for continued management. Laboratory studies are shown below. A 57-year-old immigrant from Nigeria presents to the emergency department for sudden, severe pain and swelling in her lower extremity. Serum: She was at a rehabilitation hospital when her symptoms started. HCO3-: 24 mEq/L The patient has IV drug and alcohol use disorder and has presented to the ED many times for intoxication.

She also has abdominal pain and trouble focusing that has been worsening and has lost 5 pounds recently. Ca2+: 12.5 mg/dL Her gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) has been poorly controlled recently. The patient is a non-smoker and has a history of GERD for which she takes antacids. Urea nitrogen: 12 mg/dL Nitrites: negative Red blood cells: 0/hpf Glucose: 70 mg/dL Serum: Na+: 139 mEq/L K+: 4.1 mEq/L HCO3-: 24 mEq/L Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL A physical exam is within normal limits. Laboratory studies are ordered and are below: She states she has had a cough for the past week.

A 4-year-old boy comes to the pediatrician with his mother with a 3-day history of cough and runny nose with decreased oral intake over the past 24 hours. He has no medical history or known allergies, but he has not received any of the recommended vaccines due to parental refusal. His activity level has been normal and he has been attending school until this morning. His temperature is 100.3°F (37.9°C), blood pressure is 98/62 mmHg, pulse is 85/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On examination, the child is fussy. Bilateral conjunctivae are injected, and there is redness on and around the tonsils. There is no lymphadenopathy. Faint rhonchi are heard at the lung bases bilaterally.

Her medical history is notable for depression, anxiety, and gonococcal urethritis that was appropriately treated. A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain. On physical exam, you note an athletic young woman with burly shoulders, a thick neck, and acne on her forehead and back. The pain has been dull and progressive, but became suddenly worse while she was exercising. On abdominal exam you note diffuse tenderness with 10/10 pain upon palpation of the right upper quadrant. Intravenous fluids are started and labs are sent. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 80/40 mmHg, pulse is 110/minute, and respirations are 15/minute with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. The patient's current medications include oral contraceptive pills, fluoxetine, alprazolam, ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and folate. The patient also recently lost a large amount of weight for a fitness show she planned on entering. She admits to drinking at least 5 standard alcoholic drinks a day. She is sexually active and does not use condoms. A urinary ß-hCG has been ordered.

He received a dose of the 13-valent pneumococcal vaccine and a dose of the 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine 15 years ago, as well as a second dose of the 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine 10 years ago. His temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 130/84 mmHg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 11/min. He has no concerns. His most recent lab work showed a cluster of differentiation CD4 count of 150 cells/µL. The patient is intermittently compliant with his antiretroviral therapy (ART). A 65-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a routine appointment. His past medical history is significant for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, diagnosed 15 years ago.

An 82-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency room complaining of sudden-onset, painless vision loss in his right eye starting 2 days ago. Physical exam reveals 20/800 vision in the right eye. When it started, he felt like a “curtain was pulled down” over his right eye but wasn't able to seek care immediately because it was snowing outside and he didn't want to travel in inclement weather. A fundoscopic exam of the right eye is shown in Figure A. The patient’s medications include aspirin and carvedilol. Physical and fundoscopic examinations of the left eye are unremarkable. He reports that he is a smoker with a 50-pack-year history. The patient’s temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 112/72 mmHg, pulse is 84/min, and respirations are 14/min with an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. A review of systems is significant for occasional palpitations and presyncope.

A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a headache and nausea. Upon physical examination, the right pupil is minimally responsive to light and the globe feels firm. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 135/91 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. The patient’s past medical history is significant for hypertension. When asked to indicate the area of pain, he says that it surrounds his eye and upper forehead. He had one episode of vomiting. The patient also reports difficulty seeing out of his right eye, which he attributes to excessive tearing. He states the pain is constant and is primarily located on his right side. His medications include hydrochlorothiazide. He reports that he was rocking his grandson to sleep when the symptoms began. The patient’s right eye is shown in Figure A. A right-sided carotid bruit is appreciated.

Owing to the concern for esophageal perforation, a barium swallow was performed, showing no extravasation of contrast.A, Computed tomographic scan shows extensive soft tissue inflammation in the left neck (arrowhead). Mediastinal edema and bilateral pleural effusions were also seen on computed tomographic scan (Figure, B). B, Computed tomographic scan shows bilateral pleural effusions (red arrowheads) and mediastinal edema (white arrowhead). No overlying skin changes or crepitus were appreciated. Laboratory data revealed leukocytosis (white blood cell count, 18 000/µL; to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001). There was no recent history of trauma to the neck or chest.Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and soft tissue swelling over the left supraclavicular area. . A 62-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe substernal pain radiating to the left shoulder and back and subsequent swelling of the left side of her neck. She had been recently treated at an outpatient facility for a viral illness with multiple episodes of forceful coughing. A computed tomographic scan demonstrated extensive edema of the left neck, with fat stranding seen in the subcutaneous tissues extending into the left jugular, carotid, and esophageal spaces (Figure, A).

A 59-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to a 3-month history of “always feeling the urge to urinate” as well as vaginal pruritis. The vaginal mucosa also has a loss of rugae and several areas of friable irritation. On physical examination, the vulvar skin is pale and atrophic with reduced elasticity and multiple areas of petechiae. It is not associated with coughing or sneezing. Urinalysis is normal and fecal occult blood test is negative. She has no other significant medical history and does not take any medications. She states that she has had involuntary loss of urine about 4 times each day over the past 3 months. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a small, retroverted uterus. The patient has not been sexually active with her husband due to pain with intercourse. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. There is minimal clear vaginal discharge. She has a history of chlamydial infection in her 20's and has had 3 urinary tract infections over the past year. Menopause occurred at age 52.

He exercises twice a day, often with heavy weightlifting, and eats a high-protein diet. A 31-year-old man presents to clinic for evaluation of a 3-year history of infertility. Glucose: 110 mg/dL Creatinine: 1.3 mg/dL Alanine aminotransferase (ALT, GPT): 275 U/L He also has palpable tissue underneath his nipples bilaterally. He is sexually active with his wife and has no history of sexually transmitted infections. He reports occasional alcohol use and remote marijuana use. Total bilirubin: 0.8 mg/dL Leukocyte count: 5,300/mm^3 Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL Aspartate aminotransferase (AST, GOT): 410 U/L Platelet count: 250,000/mm^3 His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 148/90 mmHg, pulse is 84/min, and respirations are 15/min. Serum: His muscle tone is normal in his upper and lower extremities bilaterally. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His laboratory values are below: Physical exam reveals small testes and a receding hairline.

He has a history of hypertension, sickle cell anemia, and a splenectomy. A radiograph is obtained as in Figure A. He now has 8/10 pain when climbing stairs or rising from a seated position. His temperature is 97.5°F (36.4°C), blood pressure is 124/68 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 16/min. There is no point tenderness. Physical exam reveals left groin pain at the terminal ranges of hip abduction and internal rotation. He localizes the pain to the front of his groin. A 24-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with left groin pain. The pain started a year ago and has progressed. He denies any erythema or swelling. He drinks a glass of wine with dinner every night and took up scuba diving 2 months ago but otherwise does not exercise. His body mass index (BMI) is 18.1 kg/m^2.

When focusing on the pediatrician's penlight, the patient's left eye wanders. However, when the right eye is covered, the left eye refocuses on the light. His mother is concerned about his vision, as she noticed him squinting while watching television. A photograph of his eyes is shown in Figure A. The rest of his neurological exam, including extraocular movements, is within normal limits. On exam, his pupils are round and reactive to light. A 15-month-old boy presents with his mother for his well-child exam. He is able to walk alone, speak 3 words, and scribble with a crayon. He is up to date with routine vaccinations. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 80/55 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 25/min.

On physical exam, he has a 1.2 x 1.7 cm ulcer on the plantar surface of his left metatarsal head. A 52-year-old man presents to the clinic with a left foot ulcer that he noticed 6 days ago. He has a history of obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and depression. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. His current medications include metformin, aspirin, rosuvastatin, lisinopril, and fluoxetine. He has a 25-pack-year smoking history and drinks 1 glass of wine a day.

He has 4/5 left-sided weakness of the upper and lower extremities and associated pronator drift of the left upper extremity. A magnetic resonance imaging study of the brain is shown in Figure A. . At the end of the study period, 40% of individuals have replied to the survey throughout the entire period. Individuals are surveyed using a validated method and followed up in 6-month intervals for 5 years. Analyzing only those subjects who responded throughout the entire period, it is determined that opioid use disorder only minimally impairs individuals in their daily functioning. A study is performed that looks at individuals who suffer from opioid use disorder and the effect the disorder has on their daily life and functionality.

Six years ago, a white woman in her 60s was incidentally found to have chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) after being noticed to have lymphocytosis during treatment for diverticulitis. Owing to progressive disease, she was started on therapy with fludarabine and rituximab (FR) 6 months later for 4 cycles, and clinical complete remission was achieved (bone marrow assessment was not done). However, 2.5 years later she experienced disease relapse. Lymphadenopathy was noticed during the initial physical examination and imaging studies. Immunophenotyping was typical for CLL, showing expression of CD 5, CD 19, CD 23, CD 38, and dim κ light chain restriction.

A 43-year-old male patient attends a routine primary care visit where urinalysis reveals 3+ protein and 1–2 red blood cells per high-power field, with no other abnormalities. He has no symptoms, no relevant family history, and denies smoking or alcohol use. Physical examination findings are unremarkable. His vital signs include a temperature of 36.7°C (98.06°F), blood pressure of 130/82 mm Hg, and a pulse rate of 78/min.

A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic for left-sided, dull, non-radiating pain in her chest for the past month. A 12-lead electrocardiogram is unremarkable and unchanged from 3 months ago. She denies recent life changes or increased stress. The patient has a past medical history of hyperlipidemia and hypertension. Vital signs are relatively unchanged from her previous visit and reveal: Current medications include simvastatin and lisinopril. His father had a myocardial infarction, and the patient smokes one pack of cigarettes daily but denies alcohol or drug use. His medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and he is taking metformin and lisinopril. A 45-year-old male visits the clinic for a routine follow-up and reports no current health concerns. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Laboratory results are provided below. What is the most appropriate next step in this patient’s management? Vital signs are as follows: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 17/min, and blood pressure 125/82 mmHg.

A 20-year-old male presents with a 2-week history of lower back pain that began the day after assisting his grandmother with moving. Lumbar flexion elicits back pain, radiating pain, and burning sensations. A straight leg test is positive on the left. He denies any direct injury but reports intermittent radiating pain and tingling from his left lateral thigh to the medial leg and foot, which is aggravated by certain positions. Patellar reflexes are diminished (1+) on the left compared to the right (2+). The vertebral transverse processes from L1–L5 are posterior and tender on the right. On examination, the lumbar paravertebral muscles are hypertonic and tender.

She reports irregular menstrual cycles that complicate ovulation timing. A 25-year-old female seeks fertility consultation after one year of unsuccessful conception attempts with regular unprotected intercourse. Bedside pelvic ultrasound demonstrates a normal-sized uterus with mild endometrial thickening, no uterine fibroids, and antral follicle counts of 23 and 11 in the right and left ovaries, respectively. In-clinic urine pregnancy test is negative. Her medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, and she takes a prenatal vitamin. Recent records indicate hemoglobin A1c of 5.8% and previous blood pressure of 142/88. Current vital signs show: temperature 36.5°C (97.8°F), pulse 72/min, respirations 18/min, blood pressure 154/92 mmHg, and BMI 36 kg/m2. Physical examination reveals no significant findings.

His beta natriuretic peptide (BNP) level is normal, and a transthoracic echocardiogram from three months ago shows no change, with an ejection fraction of 30%. A 68-year-old man with a decade-long history of COPD presents with worsening chronic cough producing sputum and increasing shortness of breath. Currently, he is unable to climb a single flight of stairs without experiencing severe dyspnea. He denies any changes in the appearance of his phlegm.

His medical history includes seizure disorder and schizophrenia, for which he takes haloperidol. On examination, his vital signs show: temperature 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure 120/84 mmHg, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. While he shows no clear focal neurologic deficits, he lacks purposeful movement of his extremities. A 33-year-old male construction worker is brought to the emergency department with acute confusion after being found unconscious at his worksite. He underwent an appendectomy two months ago. The patient is confused and non-communicative, with sweat-soaked clothing.

During the second day of hospitalization, his condition deteriorates with the onset of bilious vomiting, increased abdominal discomfort, and two episodes of bloody stools. Physical examination reveals a markedly distended and severely tender abdomen. His vital signs show tachycardia (170 beats/minute), hypotension (65/35 mm Hg), tachypnea (32 breaths/minute), and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. A 3-month-old male infant is hospitalized for dehydration initially attributed to viral gastroenteritis, presenting with irritability and vomiting.

Rectal examination and proctoscopy demonstrate significant active bleeding at an estimated rate of 2-3 mL/min, with no evident hemorrhoids or fissures. A comatose male patient of middle age is brought to the emergency department with active rectal bleeding. A nasogastric tube insertion shows bile-stained fluid without blood. After initial resuscitation with IV fluids and blood transfusion, his vital signs stabilize. His vital signs show: pulse 110/min, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He has no known medical history. Laboratory results reveal: hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, hematocrit 30%, BUN 33 mg/dL, and normal PT/aPTT. His extremities are cold.
A 41-year-old woman with a history of shellfish allergy requires intravenous radiocontrast for a CT scan to evaluate an adrenal incidentaloma.

He demonstrates a mildly antalgic gait. Recently, he bumped his knee, but this has not affected his baseline pain during walking. A 55-year-old male visits his primary care physician due to worsening left knee pain over the past year. Physical examination reveals mild erythema and bruising of the left knee without joint tenderness or pain during passive range of motion. He is attending Alcoholics Anonymous but has had limited success. Vital signs include a temperature of 98.7°F (37°C), blood pressure of 137/88 mmHg, pulse of 65/min, respirations of 11/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. His medications include insulin, metformin, hydrochlorothiazide, and lisinopril. He reports minor symptom relief with ice and rest. The patient works as a butcher and lives with his wife.

The patient describes a progressively worsening, non-radiating, achy pain rated at 5/10, which intensifies during left hip extension. A 34-year-old woman who works as a yoga instructor seeks medical attention for left hip discomfort that began one week ago. Physical assessment reveals slightly limited hip extension range of motion, but normal bilateral lower extremity strength (5/5). The seated flexion test yields negative results, and both anterior superior iliac spines (ASIS) and posterior superior iliac spines (PSIS) are symmetrically aligned. Palpation reveals a specific point of tenderness medial to the left ASIS. She reports no relevant medical history or injury to the area.

On the right side, just medial to the scapula's medial border, there is a prominent transverse process that exhibits sharp tenderness during anterior motion testing. When the patient performs forward flexion at this level, the corresponding left transverse process demonstrates increased posterior movement. During the osteopathic structural examination, the examiner notes hypertonic and mildly tender paraspinal muscles in the lower cervical and upper thoracic regions. A 45-year-old man seeks medical attention for back pain that began two weeks ago, coinciding with increased computer work due to a major project deadline. He has no significant medical history or recent trauma.

Physical examination reveals joint hypermobility, a chest wall deformity with depression of the sternum (pectus excavatum), and a decreased upper-to-lower body segment ratio. A 19-year-old female athlete presents for sports clearance evaluation. She is currently asymptomatic but has a history of multiple spontaneous pneumothoraces.

A male hiker, aged 35, presents with headache and nausea while at 2600 meters elevation. He has a clean medical history, takes no medications, and is current with Covid-19 vaccinations. - Respiratory rate: 20 breaths/min His vital signs show: The examination reveals an alert and oriented patient who appears uncomfortable but not in acute distress. His gait is steady. - Oxygen saturation: 94% on room air - Heart rate: 85 beats/min - Temperature: 36.4°C - Blood pressure: 115/80 mm Hg Physical findings include mild peripheral and facial edema, normal respiratory exam, and no neurological deficits. His SARS-CoV-2 test is negative.

Her medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, and hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto's disease. Three months ago, she was started on oral estradiol and micronized progesterone for hot flashes, omeprazole for dyspepsia, and calcium for osteoporosis. Physical examination is unremarkable. She has not experienced any falls or fractures. On review of symptoms, she notes dry skin, occasional constipation, and mild fatigue but denies dyspepsia, depressed mood, hair loss, or weight changes. Her current medications include lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily, and levothyroxine 125 μg daily. A 52-year-old woman attends a follow-up visit for management of menopausal hot flashes. She reports improvement in her hot flashes and mood.

Physical examination reveals a mass in the right breast's lower lateral quadrant and tenderness over the thoracic spinous processes, with normal neurological findings. Breast mass biopsy confirms invasive ductal carcinoma. A 54-year-old female presents with severe, dull upper back pain of 3 months' duration that worsens at night. Thoracic spine x-ray demonstrates osteolytic lesions at T4 and T5 levels.

A root cause analysis has been conducted, including participant interviews, process review, and analysis of proximate causes and contributing factors. A patient with hairy-cell leukemia experienced a six-month delay in diagnosis after initial blood work showed pancytopenia that was not followed up.

Genetic testing confirms the presence of the JAK2 V617F mutation, and a bone marrow biopsy demonstrates megakaryocyte hyperplasia without other abnormalities. An 81-year-old woman undergoes a routine complete blood count, which reveals a platelet count of 1,200,000 per mm³ (reference range: 150,000–350,000), with normal leukocyte count and hemoglobin levels. She has been in good health overall and has no history of tobacco use. She is asymptomatic and has no prior history of bleeding, myocardial infarction, stroke, or deep-vein thrombosis.

Digital rectal examination reveals a small mass within the anal canal, and anoscopy shows an erythematous, irregular mass arising from the mucosa above the dentate line. Her medical history includes hypertension and breast cancer treated with mastectomy and radiation therapy. Additionally, she has noticed occasional mucoid discharge from the anus. A 62-year-old female presents to her primary care physician with complaints of anal bleeding. She denies pain during defecation but reports increasing episodes of constipation over the past month. She takes enalapril, has a 15-pack-year smoking history, and consumes 3-4 glasses of wine weekly. On examination, her temperature is 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, pulse is 85/min, and respirations are 18/min. She appears pale but is otherwise conversational and pleasant. She describes a 4-month history of intermittent bleeding, which has worsened over the past 2 weeks.

A 17-year-old female presents with acute onset of fever (39.0°C), headache, sore throat, dry cough, myalgias, and weakness that started two days ago. Her vital signs show blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, pulse 86/min, and respirations 18/min. Physical findings include conjunctival injection and erythema of the posterior pharyngeal wall. A rapid diagnostic test of her throat swab is positive for influenza A+B.

A 27-year-old male with a history of asthma and cocaine use arrives at the emergency department following a motor vehicle collision. He takes albuterol and ibuprofen regularly. His Glasgow Coma Scale is 9, but his airway is patent with spontaneous breathing. Following blood transfusion and hydromorphone administration, he develops acute respiratory distress with bilateral wheezing, poor air movement, hypotension (60/35 mmHg), and tachycardia (160/min). Initial vital signs show: temperature 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure 70/35 mmHg, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. After receiving IV fluids, norepinephrine, and pelvic binding, his blood pressure improves to 100/55 mmHg. The patient is successfully intubated and transferred to surgical intensive care after stabilization. Physical examination reveals pelvic instability.

Upon becoming communicative, the patient admits to taking "a few" acetaminophen pills, though her parents believe the bottle was full. A 25-year-old female is brought to the emergency department in a somnolent state after being discovered by family members next to her computer approximately 3 hours ago, with an empty pill bottle nearby. Her vital signs show: temperature 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse 82/min, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 11/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Her past medical history includes anxiety, obesity, hypertension, and polycystic ovarian syndrome. She is not currently taking any medications and has been non-compliant with prescribed exercises. The family is unable to identify the specific medication but did not bring the bottle.

Their brother, who has a “thickened heart” diagnosed at the age of 15, was advised by their cardiologist to avoid competitive sports. A 13-year-old athlete is evaluated for sports participation. The patient has played soccer without any symptoms and has no prior significant past medical history. Physical exams, including an electrocardiogram, are unremarkable.

An MRI of the right lower extremity shows increased T2 and decreased T1 signals over the right femur with periosteal elevation, multiple osteolytic areas in the femoral metaphysis, and bone marrow edema. His older sister has systemic lupus erythematosus. A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 2-week history of fever and pain in his right thigh that is causing him to limp. He is at the 40th percentile for height and 45th percentile for weight. He has a right-sided antalgic gait. His leukocyte count is 12,300/mm3 and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 40 mm/h. Examination shows swelling, tenderness, warmth, and mild erythema over the right upper thigh; range of motion is limited by pain. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. He has no history of rash or joint pain. The patient appears well. X-rays of the hips and lower extremities are unremarkable. His immunizations are up-to-date. She thinks he may have hurt himself during soccer practice.

A 16-year-old female presents with a sore throat and breathing difficulties. Today, her cough worsened and began producing yellow phlegm. She is fully vaccinated, including for Covid-19, and SARS-CoV-2 testing is negative. On examination, her temperature is 39.0°C, heart rate is 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. Examination reveals nasal congestion but no drooling. The remainder of the physical exam is unremarkable. Breath sounds are present bilaterally without wheezing or rales. She appears tired, anxious, and ill, with increased work of breathing. Audible inspiratory stridor and moderate intercostal retractions are noted, which do not improve with racemic epinephrine. She reports shortness of breath, and her mother noticed a “funny sound” with her breathing that started this afternoon. She developed cough, congestion, runny nose, low-grade fever, and body aches two days ago. She has had reduced appetite and minimal fluid intake.

A man in his mid-20s with a history of alcohol abuse presented with abdominal pain after 3 days of drinking. Her medical history reveals a recent diagnosis of mild gastroenteritis following consumption of unpasteurized milk. Her current treatment is limited to medication for mild gastroenteritis. The patient reports strict adherence to her oral contraceptive regimen, citing her demanding career as a reason for avoiding pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test confirms positive hCG levels. A 24-year-old female presents to the clinic with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, and weight gain.

On examination, a soft S4 gallop is heard during cardiopulmonary evaluation, but the rest of the physical exam is unremarkable. She has a family history of myocardial infarction; her father passed away at age 50 due to the condition. Her medications include enalapril and low-dose aspirin. A 62-year-old woman visits her physician for a routine health maintenance checkup. Six months ago, she received an influenza vaccine. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall, weighs 50 kg (110 lb), and has a BMI of 18 kg/m². She smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily and has done so for the past 18 years. She consumes 4–5 glasses of wine per day and participates in ballroom dancing twice weekly. Vital signs are normal. She emigrated from Japan 30 years ago. Two years ago, both her Pap smear and colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. Her medical history includes hypertension. Her last mammogram, performed a year ago, was normal. She reports feeling well.

A 26-year-old male with an 8-year history of HIV on combination antiretroviral therapy (viral load undetectable, CD4 count 350 cells/mm³) is evaluated after experiencing his first tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. Physical findings include neck stiffness, left-sided facial and limb weakness, conjugate gaze with symmetric reactive pupils, increased tone in left extremities, and a positive Babinski sign on the left. On examination, he is febrile with BP 120/85 mm Hg, confused, and can follow two-step commands.

She has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with a pre-pregnancy HbA1c of 10.1% (target <7.0%). Handheld ultrasound confirms fetal cardiac activity at approximately 150 beats per minute. Her current medication regimen consists solely of metformin 850 mg three times daily. Bimanual examination findings are consistent with gestational age. While the pregnancy wasn't planned, it is desired. Urinalysis shows glucosuria without proteinuria. A 33-year-old woman, G2P1, attends her initial prenatal appointment at 8 weeks of gestation. Clinical examination reveals a BMI of 35 and blood pressure of 105/72 mm Hg.

A 56-year-old male patient presents with severe right leg pain and swelling four days after undergoing a craniotomy with evacuation of a subdural hematoma. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease requiring hemodialysis for the past 2 years. He experiences chills and nausea. His pre-admission medications included insulin, enalapril, atorvastatin, and sevelamer. The right calf appears swollen, warm, and erythematous. Pain is elicited in the right calf upon dorsiflexion of the right foot. On examination, his temperature is 38.3°C (101.0°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Peripheral pulses are palpable bilaterally, and cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable.

A 59-year-old female presents to clinic with a three-month history of urinary urgency, vaginal itching, and approximately four episodes of urinary incontinence daily, unrelated to coughing or sneezing. Physical examination reveals pale, atrophic vulvar skin with decreased elasticity and petechiae. The vaginal mucosa shows loss of rugae with areas of friable irritation and minimal clear discharge. She experienced menopause at age 52 and reports pain during intercourse that has led to sexual abstinence with her husband. Her medical history includes a chlamydial infection in her twenties and three urinary tract infections in the past year. She takes no medications. Vital signs are normal. Urinalysis is normal, fecal occult blood is negative, and pelvic ultrasound shows a small, retroverted uterus.

A tender point is palpated medial to the right anterior superior iliac spine, about one-third of the distance to the midline. He reports that the pain began after standing up following a prolonged period of bending over while working in his garage. He has limited range of motion with right hip extension and is unable to lie flat on the exam table comfortably. A 51-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-day history of right hip pain. The pain worsens when he tries to stand upright or lie flat. On physical examination, his lower extremities are bilaterally neurovascularly intact. His medical history includes an appendectomy during childhood. He denies any trauma, weakness, or paresthesias, but describes the pain as achy and non-radiating.

The left acromioclavicular joint shows no resistance to springing motion, while the medial end of the left clavicle demonstrates resistance to anterior motion. A 22-year-old man seeks medical attention for mild dyspnea and pain in his anterior neck and left shoulder following a football tackle two days ago. The patient finds some relief with rest and ice application. The left lateral clavicle appears elevated compared to the right side. Physical examination reveals symmetric rib movement during respiration. The supraclavicular fossa is notably tender to palpation. The pain, which is sharp and rated 4/10 at rest, worsens with left upper extremity movement and increased breathing rate, causing mild shortness of breath.
An 18-year-old patient presents with a 6-day history of symptoms including pharyngitis, fatigue, fever, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

A 23-year-old female presents to the emergency department with episodic back pain radiating to her abdomen that began yesterday, rating it 10/10 during episodes. She takes fluoxetine. Her medical history includes asthma, anxiety, and previously treated chlamydia.

Physical examination reveals nasal flaring, costosternal retractions, and perioral cyanosis. Chest imaging shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature. The mother, aged 30, reports no significant medical history, hereditary conditions, or drug use during pregnancy. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a single S2 and a systolic ejection murmur. A male neonate, aged 2 weeks, is brought to primary care with symptoms of excessive sleepiness, feeding difficulties, and grunting. Initially healthy, the infant's condition has gradually deteriorated since birth. The liver is enlarged on abdominal palpation, and all peripheral pulses are bounding. #### **INTERVENTIONS****:** Participants were randomly assigned to continue usual care alone (guideline based, including pulmonary rehabilitation and bronchodilators; n = 157) vs usual care plus bilateral coil treatment (n = 158) involving 2 sequential procedures 4 months apart in which 10 to 14 coils were bronchoscopically placed in a single lobe of each lung. Randomized clinical trial conducted among 315 patients with emphysema and severe air trapping recruited from 21 North American and 5 European sites from December 2012 through November 2015. #### **DESIGN****,** **SETTING****,** **AND** **PARTICIPANTS****:** Among patients with emphysema and severe hyperinflation treated for 12 months, the use of endobronchial coils compared with usual care resulted in an improvement in median exercise tolerance that was modest and of uncertain clinical importance, with a higher likelihood of major complications. Further follow-up is needed to assess long-term effects on health outcomes. #### **CONCLUSIONS** **AND** **RELEVANCE****:** Other serious adverse events including pneumonia (20% coil vs 4.5% usual care) and pneumothorax (9.7% vs 0.6%, respectively) occurred more frequently in the coil group. Major complications (including pneumonia requiring hospitalization and other potentially life-threatening or fatal events) occurred in 34.8% of coil participants vs 19.1% of usual care (P = .002). The between-group difference in median change in FEV1 was 7.0% (97.5% CI, 3.4% to ∞; 1-sided P < .001), and the between-group St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score improved -8.9 points (97.5% CI, -∞ to -6.3 points; 1-sided P < .001), each favoring the coil group. #### **RESULTS****:** Among 315 participants (mean age, 64 years; 52% women), 90% completed the 12-month follow-up. Median change in 6-minute walk distance at 12 months was 10.3 m with coil treatment vs -7.6 m with usual care, with a between-group difference of 14.6 m (Hodges-Lehmann 97.5% CI, 0.4 m to ∞; 1-sided P = .02). Improvement of at least 25 m occurred in 40.0% of patients in the coil group vs 26.9% with usual care (odds ratio, 1.8 [97.5% CI, 1.1 to ∞]; unadjusted between-group difference, 11.8% [97.5% CI, 1.0% to ∞]; 1-sided P = .01). #### **MAIN** **OUTCOMES** **AND** **MEASURES****:** The primary effectiveness outcome was difference in absolute change in 6-minute-walk distance between baseline and 12 months (minimal clinically important difference [MCID], 25 m). Secondary end points included the difference between groups in 6-minute walk distance responder rate, absolute change in quality of life using the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (MCID, 4) and change in forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1; MCID, 10%). The primary safety analysis compared the proportion of participants experiencing at least 1 of 7 prespecified major complications.

Additionally, the patient reports nausea, vomiting, lack of appetite, and no bowel movements since the onset of the right lower quadrant pain. The pain is achy and radiates from her umbilicus to her right lower quadrant. A 14-year-old female presents to the emergency room with right lower quadrant pain. There is tenderness to palpation one-third of the distance from the anterosuperior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. The patient also complains of pain while actively flexing her right hip against resistance. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respiration rate is 18/min. On physical examination, her abdomen has no scars or deformities; no bowel sounds are noted. It has progressively worsened in the last 2 days after eating dinner. She reports her pain as 8 on a scale of 1 to 10.

He works approximately 51 hours weekly, seeing about 20 patients per day. His practice includes 1,051 patients, with 50% being elderly. He is physically healthy, takes no medications, and a psychiatric evaluation reveals no mental health disorders. A family physician has been experiencing increased fatigue and has made two prescription errors in the past month. However, he has been receiving more negative patient reviews online.

Their current schedule includes 60 weekly hours of standard residency duties plus a 10-hour moonlighting shift on Saturdays within their residency program. Sundays are completely free from any work or educational commitments. A resident physician in their third year, who is performing well in their program, seeks additional work experience and income to address medical school debt.

Biopsy reveals adenocarcinoma of the anal canal, with a 2.5 cm mass located 1 cm proximal to the dentate line. PET/CT reveals no signs of metastatic disease or inguinal lymph node involvement. MRI shows submucosal invasion without sphincter involvement. A 50-year-old healthy male is found to have an asymptomatic anal mass during a routine colonoscopy. The examination is otherwise normal.

After initiating treatment with beta-blockers, oxygen, nitroglycerin, morphine, IV fluids, and aspirin, his blood pressure drops to 80/65 mmHg. His medication regimen consists of omeprazole, insulin, metformin, lisinopril, and as-needed clonazepam. A 67-year-old man arrives at the emergency department experiencing acute dyspnea and epigastric discomfort. Initial vital signs show: temperature 99.5°F (37.5°C), heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 90/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. His medical history includes GERD, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, anxiety, glaucoma, and IBS. Following fluid bolus administration, his heart rate decreases to 80/min and blood pressure improves to 105/75 mmHg. Physical examination reveals clear lung sounds bilaterally and notable jugular venous distention, with unremarkable cardiac auscultation.

A tender point is identified anteriorly on the right at the level of C4. No cervical lymphadenopathy is noted. Cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal findings are normal. His medical history is unremarkable, and he only takes a daily multivitamin. On physical examination, there are no abnormalities in strength, sensation, reflexes, or range of motion. He mentions experiencing neck pain since waking up this morning, which he attributes to "sleeping in an awkward position." He denies any other symptoms. A 32-year-old man comes to his primary care physician for an annual physical examination.

Physical examination reveals white spots on the temporal aspects of both conjunctivae, dry skin, and a firm, non-mobile anterior midline neck mass. A 37-year-old female patient seeks medical attention for diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss occurring over six months. She denies alcohol use and smoking. Her height is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in), weight is 54 kg (120 lb), with a BMI of 18 kg/m2. A D-xylose test shows normal renal excretion levels. Her vital signs are normal.

A hospitalized patient is visited by a medical student who enters the room without following any infection prevention and control protocols. Upon leaving, the patient's nurse informs the student about the necessary precautions.
A 31-year-old professional baseball pitcher presents with increased external rotation and a 30-degree deficit in internal rotation of his throwing shoulder compared to his non-dominant side.

A woman in her 70s presented with a week of painless, rapidly progressive, edematous, necrotic papules and plaques on the extremities, buttocks, and face with sharp demarcation at the nasolabial folds and extension into the oral mucosa (Figure, A and B). A computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed parenchymal lung nodules. Notable symptoms included 4 months of extreme fatigue, 20.4 kg weight loss, and a recent episode of hematochezia. On admission, punch biopsies of the skin were performed for both histological examination and bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacterial cultures (Figure, C and D).A, Edematous, ulcerated pink plaques confluent on forehead and cheeks with sharp demarcation at nasolabial fold are shown. Her medical history included diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension that were well controlled with simvastatin, chlorthalidone, hydralazine hydrochloride, lisinopril, and verapamil hydrochloride. She had been taking these medications for 5 years with no new exposures. On hospital day 2, she developed bright red blood per rectum, necessitating transfusion. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, but laboratory evaluation revealed that she had leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hematuria, and proteinuria. Age-appropriate cancer screening was up to date. C and D, Biopsy specimen findings (hematoxylin-eosin). B, Retiform purpuric plaque is shown on the left leg with overlying desquamation. .

A 61-year-old male patient comes to the family medicine clinic for his annual checkup. His medical history includes chronic hypertension and osteoarthritis, for which he takes lisinopril and aspirin. On physical examination, his heart rate is 76/min, respiratory rate is 16/min, temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. He underwent a normal colonoscopy three years ago. He has truncal obesity with a BMI of 30 kg/m². Social history reveals he has been married and monogamous for 30 years, works in an office, and smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily since the age of 30. Both knees show mild osteoarthritic changes. He denies alcohol or drug use. Heart sounds are normal, and lung auscultation is clear except for wheezing on forced expiration.

A 47-year-old homeless male presents with episodes of hemoptysis, generalized muscle pain, and dyspnea. Bilateral basilar crackles are noted on lung examination. His vital signs show: temperature 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 154/94 mmHg, heart rate 89/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. He acknowledges having experienced similar symptoms previously but did not seek medical attention. Due to lack of regular medical care, his medical history is unknown.

She has started taking multiple daily naps and has experienced bed-wetting despite previous toilet training. Her vital signs show: temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, pulse 105/min, and respirations 25/min. She reports constant thirst and increased appetite, though her BMI is 18.5 kg/m^2. Urinalysis reveals the presence of glucose and ketones. She has no significant medical history, takes no medications, and denies fever, chills, or gastrointestinal symptoms. A father brings his 6-year-old daughter to the pediatrician with concerns about increased sleepiness and frequent urination.

A 30-year-old male with a history of IV drug use and methamphetamine-induced CTEPH presents to the ED with worsening abdominal pain and fever. Two weeks ago, he switched from rivaroxaban to warfarin due to insurance issues. INR: 6.2 The next available OR time is in 5 hours. The pain began periumbilically and has progressed to severe groin tenderness. ALT: 45 U/L His vital signs show temperature 102°F, BP 95/60 mmHg (baseline low), pulse 95/min, and respirations 22/min. Hemoglobin: 11 g/dL Physical examination reveals bibasilar crackles, normal cardiac exam, and RLQ tenderness with LLQ rebound tenderness. Ca2+: 9.1 mg/dL BUN: 40 mg/dL Creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL AST: 34 U/L PTT: 70 seconds PT: 40 seconds Blood type: O positive Antibody screen: Negative The surgical team has confirmed the clinical diagnosis without imaging. Glucose: 110 mg/dL WBC: 16,000/mm^3 (normal differential) Platelets: 190,000/mm^3 Na+: 137 mEq/L Cl-: 100 mEq/L K+: 3.7 mEq/L HCO3-: 23 mEq/L Laboratory findings include: Hematocrit: 35%

Abdominal ultrasound reveals a homogenous, well-demarcated, hyperechoic mass in the left lobe of the liver. A follow-up ultrasound performed three months postpartum shows an increase in the size of the mass without changes in its appearance. A 30-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 20 weeks gestation presents with abdominal discomfort and early satiety lasting several days. She denies experiencing headache, visual disturbances, cramping, or vaginal bleeding, and reports normal fetal movements. Her medical history is unremarkable.

A 37-year-old male with no significant medical history presents with an 8-week history of burning epigastric pain that occurs post-prandially and occasionally radiates to his back. He reports early satiety and postprandial bloating but denies weight loss or changes in bowel habits. His social history includes moderate alcohol consumption (1-3 beers weekly) and no smoking. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness, normal bowel sounds, and is otherwise unremarkable.

A 24-year-old woman visits her primary care physician with complaints of numbness and tingling in her legs, which began 4 months ago and are sometimes accompanied by pain. Her medical history includes type I diabetes mellitus and irritable bowel syndrome. Gait is normal, and the Romberg test is negative. She is on insulin and a multivitamin. Lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. No lower extremity edema is noted. There is no spinal tenderness, and the straight leg test is negative bilaterally. She moved into a new apartment 5 months ago. These symptoms are exercise-induced, non-positional, and improve with rest. Physical examination reveals a 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border with a regular heart rate and rhythm. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal discomfort, and changes in bowel or bladder function. Her temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 18/min. Pinprick and vibratory sensation are intact, with 1+ dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally.

On examination, he has a flat affect, facial grimacing, and sudden jerky movements in his upper extremities. A 46-year-old man is brought to his primary care provider by his wife due to depression and unusual movements. His wife reports that over the past 2 months, he has become irritable and withdrawn, a stark contrast to his previously outgoing personality. He is struggling at his job as a partner at an accounting firm, with colleagues threatening to terminate his position due to poor performance. The patient expresses fear over his unexplained mood changes and tearfully admits concern about a serious underlying issue. He met his mother once but never knew his father, who reportedly died in his 50s. He consumes a few glasses of wine weekly and has never smoked. His medical history includes hypertension, managed with lisinopril, and his family history is unknown as he was adopted. His vital signs include a temperature of 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure of 141/87 mmHg, pulse of 81/min, and respirations of 12/min.

A 70-year-old female with multiple comorbidities including hypertension, coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with a two-day history of nonbloody diarrhea (8-10 times daily). She appears lethargic with a BMI of 44 kg/m2. Vital signs show temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse 115/min, respirations 26/min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination reveals dry mucous membranes, and fingerstick glucose is normal. Her medications include furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, atorvastatin, metoprolol, metformin, and dapagliflozin.

A plain radiograph of the pelvis (Figure, right panel) showed sclerosis and joint narrowing at both sacroiliac joints as well as joint narrowing and osteophytes in the hip joints bilaterally.Plain radiographs of the hands and pelvis at presentation.Order magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joint. A 44-year-old White man presented with a 15-year history of dull midline lower back pain associated with bilateral hip pain. Results of cardiopulmonary, abdominal, neurologic, and dermatologic examinations were unremarkable.Results of laboratory testing, including complete blood cell count, basic metabolic panel, and liver function tests, were within normal limits, and results for HLA-B27 were negative. Lower back flexion was decreased with only 4-mm excursion on the modified Schober test. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 8 mm/h and C-reactive protein level was 0.5 mg/dL. Musculoskeletal examination revealed swelling of the second, third, and fifth MCP joints and second and third PIP joints bilaterally as well as decreased knee and hip range of motion with minimal knee effusions. Family history was notable for a brother with osteoarthritis, hypogonadism, and type 2 diabetes.Vital signs were within normal limits (heart rate, 92/min; blood pressure, 136/84 mm Hg; respiratory rate,  16/min; oxygen saturation, 97%; temperature, 37.0 °C). He also noted bilateral hand pain along the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints and prolonged morning stiffness lasting approximately 45 minutes. A plain radiograph of the hands (Figure, left panel) showed hook-like osteophytes at the second and third MCP joints bilaterally as well as asymmetric joint swelling in multiple MCP and PIP joints.

Autopsy reveals ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and pericardial and pleural effusions, along with an enlarged placenta. She had no prenatal care during this pregnancy, which was otherwise uncomplicated. A 27-year-old Filipino immigrant presents with a stillborn male fetus at 30 weeks' gestation. The stillborn fetus exhibits pale skin and generalized edema without visible malformations. She has a healthy 3-year-old daughter and no significant medical history.

A hospice patient, a 54-year-old female with metastatic ovarian cancer, has been managing well with morphine for her dyspnea. Her daughter contacts you reporting that the patient has become unable to get out of bed and is refusing food and fluids. While the patient remains comfortable, her daughter seeks guidance about the progression of symptoms.

On physical examination, a deep sacral sulcus is noted on the right, and a posterior inferior lateral angle is observed on the left. While the patient is in the prone position, there is springing upon compression of the lumbosacral junction. A 76-year-old male presents with a 2-month history of low back pain. His medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and ankylosing spondylitis affecting the sacroiliac joint. He is currently taking metformin and captopril.

Chronic tissue texture changes are noted from T2-T7, and decreased rib motion during inhalation is observed in ribs 1-5. Physical examination reveals absent breath sounds in the right upper lung field with clear remaining lung fields. His vital signs show: BP 124/78 mm Hg, HR 78/min, RR 17/min, and temperature 37.2°C (99.1°F). He reports experiencing occasional exertional dyspnea and chest tightness, but denies fever, chest pain, or recent infections. A well-healed 4cm surgical scar is visible on the right chest at the fifth rib level. A 52-year-old male smoker (30 pack-year history) presents for one-month post-operative follow-up after a right upper pulmonary lobectomy for non-small cell lung carcinoma.

During the osteopathic structural examination, she demonstrates cervical paraspinal muscle tenderness on palpation and restricted range of motion when sidebending and rotating to the right. A 62-year-old woman with no significant medical history seeks treatment at a clinic for neck pain that began following a car accident three days prior. The treating physician employs a technique that first reduces the patient's cervical lordosis followed by applying compression. Initial emergency department evaluation showed only muscle strains.

Urinalysis is negative, and a pregnancy test is positive. A 26-year-old woman with a history of asthma arrives at the emergency department with persistent, gnawing pain in the left lower quadrant of her abdomen that began several hours ago. There is tenderness to palpation in the left lower quadrant, but her genitourinary exam is normal. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 77/45 mmHg, pulse is 121/min, and respirations are 14/min. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and acknowledges having had multiple partners in the past year. On examination, she appears diaphoretic and uncomfortable. She denies recent travel, new foods or medications, or exposure to sick contacts. She reports mild relief with ibuprofen.
