On osteopathic structural examination, there is tenderness to palpation in the musculature of the lumbar region. The patient reports a dull, constant low back pain that began 2 weeks ago after lifting furniture. The physician places their thumbs on the transverse processes of L3 and notes their right thumb appears more posterior than the left, but this resolves when the patient arches his spine. The pain is relieved when he lies down and worsens if he sits or stands for prolonged periods of time. A 32-year-old male marathon runner with no significant past medical history presents to the clinic with low back pain.

A 70-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of shortness of breath, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema. Physical examination reveals jugular vein distention, a displaced point of maximal impulse, an S4 gallop, a holosystolic murmur, and 2+ pitting edema extending to the mid-calf. After 6 hours of treatment, his blood pressure remains low, and his serum creatinine is measured at 1.9 mg/dL. He is started on furosemide, carvedilol, and oxygen therapy. Upon arrival, his vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 100/80 mm Hg, pulse 88/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and temperature 36.5°C (97.7°F). Current medications include simvastatin and lisinopril. His medical history includes a myocardial infarction 6 years ago requiring revascularization and hypertension.

You have identified two comparable populations with similar age distributions and past medical histories. One group consists of regular aspirin users, while the other group has no history of aspirin use. In your research, you are investigating the relationship between aspirin use and hemorrhagic stroke. Your goal is to analyze and compare the cerebrovascular outcomes between these two groups.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an enlarged right atrium and right ventricle; results of contrast echocardiography were negative. A 31-year-old woman presented to clinic with decreased exercise tolerance due to shortness of breath for the past 2 weeks. Physical examination revealed a fixed split S2 and a 2/6 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. She has no chest pain but was experiencing heart palpitations a few times per week. A chest radiograph was obtained (Figure 1). She denies any significant medical history, takes only multivitamins, and mentions a childhood heart murmur that was never evaluated.On examination, her blood pressure was 125/85 mm Hg, with a heart rate of 71/min and respiratory rate of 18/min. An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with incomplete right bundle-branch block. .
A patient presents with severe knee stiffness due to osteoarthritis.

A 52-year-old male patient presents with complaints of fatigue and blurry vision for the past month, along with an unintentional weight loss of 4.5 kg (10 lb) over six months. Laboratory findings reveal a hemoglobin of 17.5 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 88 μm3, increased red cell volume, and elevated serum erythropoietin concentration. His oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.

His skin appears jaundiced. Physical examination reveals right upper quadrant tenderness, a palpable liver edge extending 4 cm below the costal margin, and pain upon pressure release in the same area. A 62-year-old man is brought to his primary care physician by his daughter after avoiding medical care for the past 10 years. No lymphadenopathy is noted. The patient has been consuming more vegetables in an attempt to alleviate his symptoms. His medical history includes chronic constipation and a 50-pack-year smoking history. He is not taking any medications. Vital signs include a temperature of 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure of 197/128 mmHg, pulse of 100/min, respirations of 17/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. HEENT examination shows poor dentition but normal sclera and extraocular movements. On review of systems, he reports difficulty defecating and blood coating his stool. He reports worsening abdominal pain that started mildly but has intensified over the past week.

Osteopathic structural examination reveals significant tenderness at the right sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, as well as moderate tenderness and restricted motion of Sibson’s fascia. At rest, the clavicles appear asymmetric bilaterally. Strength and sensation are intact (5/5), and both the empty can and Neer tests are negative. Motion testing shows reduced range of motion and pain with right arm flexion. The pain worsens with overhead lifting and began a few days ago after increasing weights during training. A 23-year-old female weightlifter presents with neck and right shoulder pain that she rates as 5/10 and describes as achy. It is minimally relieved by rest and acetaminophen and interferes with her exercise routine.

A 48-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department with severe back pain following a fall. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the mid-lower back. Her medical history includes arthritis, diabetes, and hypertension. On examination, her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 129/86 mmHg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 19/min. She reports slipping on ice while walking home, causing her to fall backward and land on both posterior iliac crests. The pain and tenderness began immediately after the fall, prompting her to call for an ambulance.

A 17-year-old girl visits her pediatrician due to the absence of menstruation. She reports developing breasts 4 years ago but has not yet had her first period. The external genitalia are normal, but the vagina ends in a blind pouch at 5 cm. Her mother began menstruating at age 13. Examination reveals Tanner stage 4 breast development, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, and minimal axillary hair. Genetic testing is performed to confirm the diagnosis. She denies abdominal pain and has no significant medical history. Her vital signs are normal: temperature 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure 110/76 mmHg, pulse 72/min, and respirations 14/min. The patient is a high school volleyball player, is single, and has no history of sexual activity. She is 5 feet 7 inches tall and weighs 116 pounds (BMI 18.2 kg/m²).

A 58-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of tremors that began in her left hand, gradually progressed to her right hand, and now interfere with eating by causing her to spill food. There is mild-to-moderate bradykinesia, reduced amplitude of finger- and foot-tapping, and moderate rigidity, worse on the right. Her spouse notes a general slowing of her movements. She demonstrates a low-amplitude, high-frequency resting tremor in both hands, more pronounced on the right, with a slight postural and kinetic component. On physical examination, she has reduced emotional expression, slow but pressured speech, and decreased spontaneity of movements. Gait shows a stooped posture and right foot dragging, but tandem gait and balance are normal. Her strength, sensation, reflexes, and coordination are intact. She denies alcohol or tobacco use and reports no sleep disturbances, hyposmia, or bowel/bladder issues. She also takes atorvastatin, levothyroxine, and insulin. Lithium was discontinued 5 years ago due to thyroid hormone changes. She also reports her handwriting has become smaller over the same period. Her medical history includes 20 years of bipolar disorder, managed with aripiprazole 30 mg daily for 4 years.

During the osteopathic structural examination, there is a distinct point of severe tenderness located just above the halfway point between the left inferior lateral angle and the left greater trochanter. Palpation of this area produces localized pain with a tingling sensation extending down the left leg, but without radiation of the primary pain. A 23-year-old female athlete with no notable medical history seeks medical attention for cramping discomfort in her posterior left thigh, which has escalated since she intensified her running routine over the last three weeks. The symptoms improve with rest but are exacerbated by running activity. She has not used any pain medication.

A 79-year-old female with chronic hypertension (managed with daily amlodipine) and anxiety disorder (treated with sertraline and lorazepam daily) is brought to evaluation by her son due to recent onset confusion. She is oriented to person but exhibits disorientation to place and time (knows the year but not month or day). The patient denies additional symptoms and confirms no recent changes to her medication regimen, including no new over-the-counter medications or supplements. Her anxiety is well-controlled, and she reports no depression. Her son also noticed uncharacteristic disorganization at her home and discovered several unpaid bills. Infectious disease workup is negative. Brain CT scan shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes, kidney and liver function tests, and urinalysis, are all within normal limits. Both neurological and physical examinations are unremarkable. Clinical examination reveals normal vital signs. The senior center manager recently contacted her son expressing concerns about her appearing confused, forgetful, and occasionally drowsy during recent book club meetings. She is a retired creative-writing instructor who maintains independent living, handles her personal affairs, and actively leads a book club at her local senior center.

On physical examination, the patient exhibits a smooth, red beefy tongue and demonstrates both sensory and motor deficits in his lower extremities. His dietary history reveals strict adherence to a vegan diet since age 18, excluding all animal products including eggs and dairy. A 26-year-old male patient from India presents to the clinic reporting persistent fatigue and low energy levels for the past few weeks. He also describes experiencing weakness and numbness in his lower extremities. He does not supplement his diet with vitamins.

A woman in her 60s with a history of bilateral proliferative diabetic retinopathy complicated by a recent vitreous hemorrhage in her left eye presented with an acute onset of redness, irritation, and blurred vision in her left eye. Her symptoms started 1 day after she rubbed her left eye with her hands after handling the milky latex (a fluid found in 10% of flowering plants) of a plant in her garden. On anterior segment examination, she was found to have pinpoint epithelial defects, thickened stroma, and dense Descemet folds, along with a nuclear sclerotic cataract (Figure 1). A posterior pole examination was limited by corneal edema, but there was evidence of a vitreous hemorrhage. She had no recent history of recent eye surgery, eye trauma, cold sores, or new illnesses.On presentation, her visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/200 OS. The fellow eye had no corneal edema and was pseudophakic, with prior panretinal photocoagulation scars in the peripheral retina. Central pachymetry in the left eye measured 706 μm, which was elevated from the mean expected pachymetry values of 540 to 560 μm. Her intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg OD and 19 mm Hg OS. Her pupils were equal, round, and reactive in both eyes. .

A 72-year-old female presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and a 5-day history of bloody diarrhea that has progressively worsened. Her medical history includes ulcerative colitis, hypertension, and hypothyroidism, with current medications being hydrochlorothiazide, levothyroxine, and sulfasalazine. In the past 24 hours, she has developed fevers and chills. - Blood pressure: 90/60 mmHg - Temperature: 39.1°C (102.4°F) The patient is oriented to person and place but not time. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Physical examination reveals dry mucous membranes, an unremarkable cardiopulmonary exam, and a distended, tender abdomen without rebound tenderness. - Respirations: 20/min - Pulse: 120/min Vital signs show:

Ribs 2–5 on the right show poor elevation during inhalation but descend normally with exhalation. On physical examination, heart and lung sounds are normal, but there is localized tenderness over the right anterior rib cage and restricted sidebending of T1–T6 to the right. A 29-year-old female presents with a 10-day history of upper back pain on the right side. Vital signs are normal. She denies any recent trauma but mentions that her new job requires prolonged sitting. Her medical history includes intermittent tension headaches.

A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 3-week history of constant low back pain that began after the birth of her second child. The sacral bases are symmetrically anterior, and moderate springing of the sacrum is noted with an anterior force. Physical examination reveals no tenderness in the thoracic or lumbar regions. She has no additional symptoms and reports that her baby is healthy and exclusively breastfed. The pain worsens with forward and backward bending. Both the standing and seated flexion tests are equivocal.

The patient is treated conservatively with a collar and cuff sling, with instructions that the fracture will heal naturally with proper immobilization. A 19-year-old male presents to the emergency department following a motorcycle accident with complaints of pain and numbness in his right arm. Clinical examination and imaging studies confirm a proximal humerus fracture.

The patient is to be treated with a technique that engages the restrictive barrier of the key rib by employing a single brief, rapid force over a short distance. Ribs 5–9 on the right do not rise with the left. A 43-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of difficulty breathing that has gradually been increasing for the past 2 weeks. He has no history of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Structural exam reveals asymmetric rib motion on inhalation. Lung sounds are equal bilaterally with no rales, wheezes, or rhonchi. On examination, the heart has a regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. He states the difficulty breathing is due to intermittent sharp pains that are worse when exercising. He denies edema, cough, shortness of breath, and orthopnea. A 12-lead electrocardiogram is taken and shows a P wave to every QRS complex, a rate of 76 beats per minute, a constant PR interval, and QRS complexes consistent at about 90 ms wide.

His vital signs show: temperature 104°F (40°C), blood pressure 147/88 mmHg, pulse 200/min, respirations 33/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He was also treated for several seemingly similar lesions on the face and scalp and had a family history of similar cutaneous lesions reported in 2 brothers and 1 niece.Figures show crusted erythematous papules and plaques adjacent to the surgical excision scar within a prior irradiation field on the head and neck (A) and erythematous and hyperpigmented papules and plaques overlying diffuse postsurgical scarring within a prior irradiation field on the back (B). A white man in his 20s presented with numerous pink and brown papules and plaques, some with ulceration, on the head and along the midline of the neck and spine (Figure). Medical history included medulloblastoma treated with irradiation of the brain and spine at age 2 years. . He also received radiation therapy for a meningioma of the posterior fossa in adulthood.

DNA purified from the leukocytes of the patient is reacted in a mixture containing oligonucleotides specific for CMV DNA, thermostable DNA polymerase, and nucleotides. A technician wants to determine whether cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA is present in the blood of a bone marrow transplant recipient. Repetitive cycles of heating and cooling are performed, and the reaction product is detected by gel electrophoresis.

A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his babysitter because of a 30-minute history of respiratory distress. Oxygen saturation is now 93%. The child's mother, who is a single parent, is currently out of town for business but will return later tonight. The babysitter reports that she is 15 years old and has cared for the patient on numerous occasions during the past year. Despite continued supplemental oxygen and hydration, the child remains tachypneic and stridorous at rest. The babysitter says, "He has had a runny nose since I started babysitting yesterday, but this afternoon he awoke from a nap with a barking sound and he was breathing real heavy." Treatment with 40% oxygen via venturi mask and intravenous fluids is initiated. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Auscultation of the chest discloses equal air entry on both sides and no crackles. Physical examination discloses inspiratory stridor. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 89%. Neck is supple, tympanic membranes are normal, and there is a profuse nasal discharge. He is obviously comfortable with his caregiver. The child looks tired and sits upright on the babysitter's lap. Examination of the pharynx discloses no abnormalities. She does not know the child's prior health history, nor does she know if the boy takes any medications on a regular basis. Vital signs are temperature 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse 110/min, respirations 28/min and labored, and blood pressure 85/50 mm Hg.

A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting; he also has had decreased appetite during this period. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a perforated appendix. Abdominal examination shows guarding with diffuse rebound tenderness. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 143/83 mm Hg. The pain was initially on the right but now has become generalized. There are no palpable masses.

A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of low-grade fever and increasing abdominal cramps that are exacerbated by bowel movements. The abdomen is soft, and there is tenderness to palpation of the left lower quadrant with guarding but no rebound. She began a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate and metronidazole 2 days ago but has had no relief of her symptoms. She has not had nausea, vomiting, urinary symptoms, or bloody stools. The stool is brown, and test for occult blood is negative. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. She has had intermittent constipation for the past 12 years. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2 . Her hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dL, leukocyte count is 15,000/mm3 , and platelet count is 280,000/mm3 ; serum studies and urinalysis show no abnormalities. Bowel sounds are normal. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 150/80 mm Hg. She has a 3-year history of hypertension. She underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 5 years ago because of leiomyomata uteri. The lungs are clear to auscultation.

Her mother died of colon cancer, and her maternal grandmother died of breast cancer. A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of vaginal bleeding for 2 to 5 days every 2 weeks. Menses previously occurred at regular 25- to 29-day intervals and lasted for 5 days with normal flow. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2 . The uterus is normal sized. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms inconsistently. The ovaries cannot be palpated. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The flow varies from light to heavy with passage of clots. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative.

A 13-year-old girl is brought to the office for a health maintenance visit. You have been the patient's physician for the past 6 years and know she is prepubescent. During today's visit, her mother reports that the girl has been talking about babies. She was diagnosed with Turner syndrome in infancy during a work-up for coarctation of the aorta.

He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation. A 77-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a 12-hour history of word-finding difficulty and weakness and sensory loss of the right arm and leg. His pulse is 80/min and irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 170/90 mm Hg. Current medications include metformin, lisinopril, and aspirin. There is moderate weakness and decreased sensation of the right upper and lower extremities. His serum glucose concentration is 162 mg/dL. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. He follows commands but has nonfluent aphasia. He is alert. He has no history of similar symptoms. Babinski sign is present on the right.

On morning rounds you note that the delivery records report that she had mildly elevated blood pressure during labor and sustained an estimated third-stage blood loss of 500 mL. The uterine fundus is firm and at the level of the umbilicus, and her perineum is slightly edematous. A 16-year-old high school student, whose prenatal course you have managed, delivers a 3256-g (7-lb 3-oz) baby girl during the night with the assistance of your associate. Today blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg, she is afebrile, and deep tendon reflexes are normal. She is cuddling her infant and normal bonding seems to be occurring. Hematocrit is 33%.

Her sister has asthma. A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of exercise-induced cough and nasal congestion. Her pulse is 68/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/75 mm Hg. She has not had chest pain or palpitations. The cough is nonproductive and resolves with rest. She plays field hockey and has noticed she coughs when running up and down the field. The patient appears well. Spirometry shows an FEV1:FVC ratio of 90% and an FEV1 of 90% of predicted. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. She takes no medications and does not smoke. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities.

Examination of the left lower extremity shows a 7-cm, pink, soft, granular, edematous wound. One week ago, she was treated in the emergency department after she accidentally spilled hot grease on her left leg while working at a fast-food restaurant. A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination.

B, Color fundus photograph demonstrating Frisén grade 2 optic disc edema associated with subretinal fluid, exudate, and retinal hemorrhages.Perform a lumbar puncture with opening pressure, routine chemistry, and cell count analysis. A woman in her 20s was referred to the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Neuro-Ophthalmology Service with a 2-month complaint of frequent headaches and 1 week of blurry vision in her left eye. On review of systems, she endorsed nausea as well as paresthesia in her hands.Neuro-ophthalmic examination revealed visual acuities of 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS, with no pinhole improvement. Applanation tonometry revealed pressures of 16 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. Results from brain magnetic resonance imaging with magnetic resonance venography with and without contrast were normal.A, Color fundus photograph demonstrating Frisén grade 2 optic disc edema. Color vision (Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates) was within normal limits bilaterally, although it was noted to be slightly slower in the left eye. Her current medications included hydrochlorothiazide and fluoxetine. Her medical history revealed systemic hypertension, depression, and obesity. Automated (Humphrey) visual field testing revealed enlargement of the blind spot in the right eye (mean deviation, −2.91 dB) and generalized, nonspecific depression in the left eye (mean deviation, −3.41 dB). Slitlamp examination revealed no cells in the anterior chamber or the anterior vitreous in either eye. Her ocular history was significant only for refractive error. Pupils were symmetric with slow responses bilaterally but without afferent defects. Examination of her fundus was notable for bilateral optic disc swelling (Frisén grade 2 in each eye) as well as unilateral macular exudates, subretinal fluid, and subretinal hemorrhages in the left eye (Figure 1). With the Amsler grid, she reported significant metamorphopsia in the left eye.

Her brother and maternal uncle had Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and died at the ages of 28 and 17 years, respectively. The patient's 50-year-old mother has a serum muscle creatine kinase concentration of 300 U/L. Serum studies show a muscle creatine kinase concentration of 120 U/L (N=22– 198). Genetic analysis was not performed on either relative prior to death. A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician for genetic counseling prior to conception.

A 3-year-old white girl is brought to the office by her parents for a follow-up visit 48 hours after receiving a 5-TU PPD skin test. Physical examination shows 10 mm of induration at the puncture site; the examination is otherwise normal. The parents tell you they are shocked by this finding since both of their skin tests were nonreactive. The test was done as part of a routine screening for enrollment in a homeless shelter. Until moving into this shelter they had been "squatters" in vacant buildings. She has not had much medical care in the past 2 years but she has been healthy. They say they were born in this country and tell you that their daughter has always been in good health.

She subsequently develops urinary incontinence. There is no evidence of urinary tract infection and no prior history of urinary pathology. A 65-year-old female is admitted to the hospital after experiencing aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis.

The patient asks the physician to order the MRI indicating that she has neurologic findings. She has no history of major medical illness. Musculoskeletal and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. A 35-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-day history of severe right back pain. She has not had any fever, chills, or weight loss. When told that her examination is normal, the patient becomes tearful and demands an MRI of her back because her mother just died from breast cancer metastatic to bone and she fears that she may also have cancer. The patient already contacted her insurance company, who told her that if she has neurologic abnormalities an MRI may be covered by her plan.

A plain x-ray shows a fracture of the superior pubic ramus and retrograde urethrography is done to evaluate for a urethral disruption. A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being struck by a car while driving his motorcycle. On examination, there is bruising of the perineum and pain is elicited with motion of his pelvis. There is no other penile trauma. Blood is noted at the urethral meatus. He reports severe pelvic pain.

In a subsequent malpractice suit, the plaintiff establishes that the sponge could not have been left unless there was negligence. After the scan is complete, the radiologist calls to report that the patient has a surgical sponge in her pelvis. Following a physical examination, a CT scan of the pelvis is ordered. A 33-year-old female presents to the office with the complaint of chronic pelvic pain that began after she underwent a hysterectomy 6 months ago.

A 35-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up of sarcoidosis. His only new complaint is pain in his legs that increases with weight-bearing. There is mild left hip pain present with both active and passive range of motion. Dorsalis pedis pulse is intact. Neurologic examination is normal. The patient is thin and is in no acute distress. Auscultation of the chest discloses scattered bilateral basilar crackles. Vital signs now are temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 78/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. He has been taking glucocorticoid therapy for the past 6 months.

The patient's daughter, who is visiting the patient, says he has had increased lethargy for the past day and decreased ambulation during the past 6 months. Auscultation of the chest discloses rhonchi in the right mid lung field. Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. Vital signs are temperature 38.9°C (102.0°F), pulse 60/min supine and 68/min standing, respirations 22/min, and blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg supine and 80/50 mm Hg standing. He is fully oriented but lethargic. The patient appears ill and older than his stated age. Appropriate intravenous antibiotic therapy is initiated. ECG shows no abnormalities. Medical history is also remarkable for hypertension. Abdominal examination discloses no abnormalities. A 67-year-old man with Parkinson disease is admitted to the hospital for treatment of pneumonia. Medications include hydrochlorothiazide, atenolol, levodopa, and carbidopa. He is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 78 kg (172 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m2 . Neurologic examination discloses masked facies, bradykinesia, and cogwheel rigidity; gait was not assessed on admission. She also says that there are times during the day when his tremors increase in severity, although he continues to care for himself at home.

A 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of increasing shortness of breath, sore throat, and a cough productive of a small amount of white phlegm. Over the past week, she has had nausea related to excess coughing. Over the past year, she has had a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss. Examination shows a 2-cm, nontender lymph node in the right supraclavicular area. A CT scan of the chest shows a 7.5 x 7.5 x 6-cm right lower lobe mass with some scattered calcifications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 44 years and drinks one alcoholic beverage daily. The lesion abuts the posterior chest wall without clear invasion. There are right lower peritracheal, precarinal, right hilar, and subcarinal lymph nodes. There is a 1.5-cm mass in the right adrenal gland. Examination shows no other abnormalities. She appears thin. An x-ray of the chest shows a large right lower lobe density. She has asthma treated with theophylline and inhaled β-adrenergic agonists and corticosteroids.

A 46-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the office because of a 2-week history of black discharge from her right nipple. There is scant, black discharge from the right nipple. The studies showed likely benign findings with recommended follow-up in 6 months. The patient had mammography and ultrasonography of the breasts 2 months ago for evaluation of increased glandularity, palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, noted at her most recent annual examination. Palpation of the right breast discloses glandularity in the upper outer quadrant but no other masses. Vital signs are normal. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable and she takes no medications. BMI is 30 kg/m2 .

C, Nonseptate hyphae with round terminal sporangia and free spores (lactophenol cotton blue mount; original magnification ×400). B, Broad nonseptate hyphae surrounding and infiltrating dermal blood vessels (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×400). Of note, occasional septae are seen in this specimen, consistent with the characteristic finding that mucormycetes are pauciseptate, rather than aseptate, molds. Punch biopsy specimens were obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B) and fungal culture (Figure, C).A, Gray-violet plaque on posterior upper arm at site of adhesive portion of bandage. A 4-year-old girl with newly diagnosed acute lymphocytic leukemia, receiving her initial course of chemotherapy with vincristine, daunorubicin, and methotrexate, developed a painful lesion on her left triceps. The tender area was beneath an adhesive bandage placed where she had received DTaP (diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis) and polio vaccinations 3 weeks earlier. White blood cell and neutrophil counts were low at 0.4 K/μL (normal range, 4.86-13.18 K/μL) and 0.18 K/μL (normal range, 1.60-8.29 K/μL), respectively. . Blood culture findings were negative. Otherwise, she appeared remarkably well, and her vital signs were normal. Removing the bandage revealed a tender indurated gray-violet plaque (Figure, A).

A 37-year-old woman with AIDS comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressive diarrhea and a 1.8- kg (4-lb) weight loss. During the past week, she has had six large watery stools daily. She is employed as a flight attendant and works regularly on domestic flights throughout the USA. The abdomen is scaphoid. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 112/64 mm Hg. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 400/mm3 (Normal≥500). She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2 . She also flies to Asia at least once monthly. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. She is currently receiving triple antiretroviral therapy.

A healthy 22-year-old man participates in a study of glucose metabolism. Twelve hours later, his serum glucose concentration remains within the reference range. He then sleeps through the night without additional food or drink. At the beginning of the study, his serum glucose concentration is within the reference range. He consumes an 800-calorie meal consisting of protein, fat, and carbohydrates.

A lumbar puncture is done; cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows an erythrocyte count of 340/mm3 , a leukocyte count of 121/mm3 (88% monocytes), and a protein concentration of 78 mg/dL. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). She has had a headache, cough, and fever for 3 days treated with acetaminophen and dextromethorphan. Neurologic examination shows diffuse hyperreflexia. On mental status examination, she is confused and has short-term memory deficits. A previously healthy 22-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department by her parents 20 minutes after they observed her having a seizure. She has difficulty naming objects and makes literal paraphasic errors. After the seizure, she was confused and had difficulty thinking of some words. An MRI of the brain shows bitemporal hyperintensities.

A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of increased facial hair growth. Her serum testosterone concentration is increased. Serum concentrations of androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, and urinary 17-ketosteroids are within the reference ranges. Pelvic examination shows clitoral enlargement. Her pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m2 . Physical examination shows temporal balding and coarse dark hair on the upper lip and chin. Her last menstrual period was 4 months ago. Ultrasonography of the pelvis shows a 12-cm ovarian mass.

A 77-year-old female presents to the office for evaluation of a syncopal event that occurred while she was walking. There is radiation of the murmur into the neck. Cardiac examination reveals a grade 3/6 systolic murmur, heard best at the right upper sternal border.

All the toes on the right foot have turned black. Examination discloses cellulitis in the midfoot. Three weeks ago a 45-year-old man was admitted to the hospital because of frostbite of both feet. He has become slightly febrile and progressively more confused during the past few days. He was treated by rapid rewarming and protective care of the feet.

A 35-year-old man comes to the office because of 1-week history of mid low back pain that radiates down his right leg. The pain began after the patient lifted a heavy box onto his truck. Straight-leg raise test is positive on the right, with loss of right ankle reflex. Medical history is unremarkable and he takes no medications. He rates his current pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. He has been unable to find a comfortable position and has been sleeping in a recliner. BMI is 27 kg/m2 . He appears uncomfortable and stands during the physical examination. Vital signs are normal. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 25 years, and he drinks a six-pack of beer on Friday and Saturday nights.

Examination of the right forearm shows edema around a fluctuant erythematous lesion at the site of trauma. A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and swelling of his right arm where he scraped it on a tree branch 2 days ago. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). The area is extremely tender to palpation.

She had a normal Pap smear 3 months ago and saw her ophthalmologist 6 months ago. She has a 2-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus controlled with insulin. Her 67-year-old grandmother has breast cancer. A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician in October for a follow-up examination. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2 . Her hemoglobin A1c is 6.2%, and fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 118 mg/dL. She feels well.

A 42-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. The patient is upset that his hand has not fully healed, and he files a malpractice suit against the physician. Physical examination shows decreased range of motion in the affected hand. Four months ago, he underwent repair of a Dupuytren contracture.

A 19-day-old Japanese male infant presented with a 12-day history of fevers and facial rash. Laboratory investigation showed a white blood cell count of 10.5 ×103/µL (reference range, 4.8-18.5 ×103/μL); hemoglobin level, 7.2 g/dL (8.7-13.5 g/dL); platelet count, 47 × 104/µL (28-91 ×104/μL); aspartate aminotransferase level, 23 IU/L (20-62 IU/L); alanine aminotransferase level, 9 IU/L (11-45 IU/L); serum creatinine level, 0.27 mg/dL (0.12-0.27 mg/dL); uric acid level, 2.6 mg/dL (1.8-5.3 mg/dL); and C-reactive protein level, 6.94 mg/dL (<0.30 mg/dL).Scattered annular erythematous plaques with central atrophy and raised margin on the forehead and periorbital areas of patient.Provide education on proper facial cleansing and moisturizingOrder antinuclear antibody, anti-Ro/SS-A, and anti-La/SS-B antibody testing for both the infant and his motherOrder a serologic test for syphilis for the infant. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. He was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 36 weeks’ gestational age with a birthweight of 3048 g (6.7 lb) with Apgar scores of 9 and 10. There were no complications during the prenatal and perinatal periods. His family history was unremarkable.On examination, he had a temperature of 38.0°C, a heart rate of 150/min, and a respiratory rate of 60/min. His mother had no history of ringworm infection, positive IgG antibodies against rubella virus and herpes zoster virus, and serology findings negative for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, and syphilis. Slightly scaly annular erythematous plaques with central atrophy and raised margins were present on the forehead and periorbital areas (Figure).
During a study of renal glomeruli, a healthy animal kidney is kept in a vascular bath preparation at a constant afferent arterial pressure of 100 mm Hg.

A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 0, aborta 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the office for a prenatal visit. Her blood group is O, Rh-negative. The father's blood group is B, Rh-positive. Fetal ultrasonography shows a male fetus with no abnormalities. Today, her vital signs are within normal limits. She has had one previous pregnancy resulting in a spontaneous abortion at 12 weeks' gestation. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 28-week gestation.

A 46-year-old man with Marfan syndrome, aortic insufficiency, and mitral regurgitation comes to the emergency department because he has had severe substernal chest pain for the past 3 hours. He describes the pain as tearing in quality and radiating to the neck. One week earlier he experienced similar but less severe chest pain and treated himself with aspirin.

A 47-year-old man is admitted to the hospital through the emergency department because of the sudden onset of palpitations, left-sided chest pain, light-headedness, and shortness of breath that began while he was watching television 2 hours ago. Medical history is remarkable for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The patient was given oxygen via nasal cannula and intravenous metoprolol 5 mg every 5 minutes for a total of 15 mg. His pulse slowed to 90/min. ECG obtained in the emergency department showed atrial fibrillation with narrow QRS complex. Physical examination was remarkable for rapid heart rate. Blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. Pulse was 146/min. Two hours after admission, he is pain free but his pulse is now 160/min. The patient is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2 .

A 73-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of diffuse weakness and tingling of her arms and legs. Neurologic examination shows weakness of the extensor and flexor muscles of the lower extremities. Sensation to vibration and position is decreased in all extremities, but the decrease is more prominent in the lower extremities than in the upper extremities. Knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes are exaggerated.

Over 1 year, a study is conducted to assess the antileukemic activity of a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis. All patients enrolled in the study are informed that they would be treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor. They are assigned to successive dose cohorts of 300 to 1000 mg/day of the drug. Treatment efficacy is determined based on the results of complete blood counts and bone marrow assessments conducted regularly throughout the study. Six to eight patients are assigned to each dose.

Despite therapy, he continues to have chest pain and shortness of breath. He rates the chest pain as a 7 on a 10-point scale and notes that the pain is radiating down his left arm. The patient is fully oriented. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Auscultation of the heart discloses an audible S1 and S2. There is no edema, cyanosis, or clubbing of the digits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he developed chest pain and shortness of breath 1 hour ago, shortly after snorting cocaine for the first time. Medical history is unremarkable and the patient takes no medications or any other illicit drugs. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2 . Vital signs are temperature 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse 110/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 200/100 mm Hg. Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation. Lungs are clear to auscultation and percussion. He is treated with supplemental oxygen, a 325-mg aspirin tablet, and intravenous nitroglycerin and lorazepam. The patient is diaphoretic.

Results of the trial showed no overall benefit of the vaccine. However, post hoc analysis disclosed a small but statistically significant vaccine protection among African American subjects. A phase 2, multicenter trial was conducted to determine the efficacy of a new vaccine for prevention of HIV infection. The study enrolled 4000 subjects, aged 20 to 65 years. Of these subjects, 2100 were men and 1900 were women; 2500 were white, 1000 were African American, 300 were Hispanic, and 200 were Asian/Pacific Islanders.

A nurse alerts you that he noticed a faint odor of alcohol near the physician. When approached, the physician appears tired and more disheveled than usual. There is an odor of alcohol on his breath. The physician was recently hired and has had no actions on his license by any state medical board. A 33-year-old male physician reports for a shift in the emergency department. He is married with three children, and his wife is pregnant with twins. He is a skilled and talented physician with no known history of substance or alcohol use disorder.

Examination shows a 6-cm, soft, nontender left scrotal mass that transilluminates; there are no bowel sounds in the mass. A 22-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He has had a painless left scrotal mass since childhood. Examination of the testis shows no abnormalities. He feels well.

For the past year, the patient had been investigated for hypochromic microcytic anemia. Further investigation involved capsule endoscopy, which was ingested 3 days prior to his emergency department admission. Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic computed tomography demonstrated a small-bowel obstruction, with a transition zone located at the mid-jejunum. Results of routine laboratory testing were essentially normal except for a low level of hemoglobin (8.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]), with no leukocytosis noted. Adjacent to this area, the endoscopic capsule (asterisk) is demonstrated in a proximal dilated loop of the small bowel. As part of the investigation, he underwent an esophagogastroduodenoscopy and a colonoscopy, which revealed a normal-looking bowel with no obvious source of bleeding visualized. . Adjacent to this area, the capsule was clearly demonstrated in a dilated proximal loop of the small bowel (Figure 1).Computed tomographic scan showing an intraluminal hypodense mass (pink arrowhead) causing a small-bowel obstruction. The patient claimed not to have passed a bowel movement containing the capsule. An intraluminal hypodense mass was demonstrated in this area and appeared to be the cause of the obstruction. Physical examination results were normal except for a nontender distended and tympanic abdomen. A 43-year-old man with generally good health presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of cramps and abdominal pain.

Cultures of the aspirate grow yellow, βhemolytic colonies that are catalase and coagulase positive. A polymerase chain reaction test shows mecA-positive organisms. Examination of a fine-needle aspirate from one of the nodes shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. A 3-year-old boy with chronic granulomatous disease is brought to the physician because of a 3-week history of fever and warm, red lumps under both arms. Physical examination shows enlarged, 3-cm, erythematous axillary lymph nodes bilaterally. On palpation, the nodes are tender, fluctuant, and movable. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F).

He had an episode of anaphylaxis secondary to latex allergy during a previous operation for functional expansion of his bladder through a bowel anastomosis. The patient is paraplegic, has recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones, and recent onset of incontinence secondary to detrusor and bladder neck dysfunction. A 35-year-old man with spina bifida is admitted to the hospital for a urologic procedure. Aside from paraplegia, lower extremity muscle atrophy, and lower abdominal surgical scars, the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. He has maintained continence through periodic self-catheterization. Physical examination shows a well-developed, well-nourished man in no acute distress. He has been functionally independent in activities of daily living and is employed doing inventory control in a local sporting goods store. Vital signs are normal.

The swelling has never been red or "stuck." A right inguinal hernia is confirmed on physical examination. Vital signs are normal. A 6-month-old male Hispanic infant is brought to the office by his parents because of intermittent swelling of his right scrotum that is more pronounced when he cries.

A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of dizziness for 6 weeks. An ECG shows sinus bradycardia with no evidence of ischemia. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her pulse is 55/min. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg in the right arm and 70/50 mm Hg in the left arm while supine; her blood pressure is 70/50 mm Hg in the right arm and 50/30 mm Hg in the left arm immediately after standing. Carotid duplex ultrasonography shows reverse flow in the left vertebral artery with no evidence of occlusion. A 33-year-old man undergoes a radical thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer. She characterizes these attacks as episodes of weakness and loss of feeling in her legs for several minutes. During one of these episodes, she became incontinent. A 44-year-old woman with a 10-year history of arthritis comes to the office because she has had increasing pain and stiffness in her hands, wrists, and knees during the past several months. She has seen numerous physicians for her arthritis in the past and has tried various medications and devices, including copper bracelets from Mexico given to her by friends. She says, "I had several drop attacks during the past 3 months." Review of her medical records confirms that the initial diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is correct. Physical examination shows facial plethora and swollen and painful metacarpophalangeal and knee joints, bilaterally. There is moderate ulnar deviation of the fingers. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. She currently takes aspirin approximately four times daily and ibuprofen occasionally. She also has had increasing fatigue for the past month, along with a weight loss of 1.8 to 2.2 kg (4 to 5 lb).

Three days after hospitalization for diabetic ketoacidosis, an 87-year-old woman refuses insulin injections. She accurately describes her medical history and understands the consequences of refusing insulin. There is no evidence of depression. She dismisses any attempts by the physician to change her mind, saying that the physician is too young to understand her situation. On mental status examination, she is alert and cooperative. She has no family and most of her friends are sick or deceased. She says that her medical condition has declined so much that she no longer wishes to go on living; she is nearly blind and will likely require bilateral leg amputations. She reports that she has always been an active person and does not see how her life will be of value anymore.

An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, and itchy eyes. Physical examination shows conjunctival injection and discharge and oropharyngeal erythema. He has no history of major medical illness and receives no medications. He just returned from a weeklong summer camp that included hiking trips and swimming lessons in the camp-owned swimming pool. His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. He appears tired. The public health department reports an outbreak of similar symptoms among the other campers and camp volunteers.

Medical history is significant for esophageal varices secondary to alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites treated with spironolactone. He drinks eight to ten alcoholic beverages daily. A 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has felt nauseated and light-headed for the past hour. Vital signs are temperature 36.0°C (96.8°F), pulse 110/min, respirations 12/min, and blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg. While you are obtaining additional history, the patient vomits a large volume of bright red blood and becomes difficult to arouse.

He is sitting upright and appears catatonic. A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being found with a "blank stare" and flat facial expression at a party. Physical examination shows rigidity. During the examination, he becomes hostile and attempts to assault the physician. His pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg.

She says the urinary symptoms typically begin a few days before she is going to fly and they stop the day after she arrives at her destination. A 24-year-old recent college graduate comes to the office because of a 3-year history of increased frequency of urination and occasional incontinence whenever she travels. She says she is anxious about flying and even slightly "panicky." She reports having had similar but milder symptoms prior to examinations before graduating. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. Vital signs are normal. Urinalysis and urine culture are normal. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities.

A healthy 2-year-old girl is brought to the office for a routine well-child visit. The child was weaned at 6 months of age and began to walk at 10 months of age. On physical examination, she has mild bowlegs (10-degree genu varum).

A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of episodes of fainting for 3 months. His pulse is 40/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/85 mm Hg. He had a myocardial infarction 12 years ago. Physical examination shows evidence of cannon a waves. He also has had difficulty performing daily tasks because he is easily fatigued. An ECG shows a P-wave rate of 90/min, and an R-wave rate of 40/min, with no apparent relation between the two.

Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 2900/μL (80% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 0% eosinophils, and 0% basophils); hemoglobin level, 15.2 g/dL; and platelet count, 187 ×103/μL. He did not smoke and only drank alcohol occasionally. A maculopapular rash was noted on the trunk and extremities (Figure) as well as the palms and soles. . Serum electrolyte levels were normal. The lungs were clear to auscultation. The face was not involved. He was alert and oriented. No hepatosplenomegaly was noted.

The student met the woman when he was assigned to her care during her 2-week hospitalization for treatment of major depressive disorder. He is attracted to this former patient and would be interested in dating her. He has not treated or seen the patient since she was discharged from the hospital. A 22-year-old woman contacts a medical student and asks if he would like to join her for dinner.

A 45-year-old woman has a 2-week history of increased anxiety, abdominal discomfort, irritability, and difficulty concentrating; she was robbed at knifepoint in a parking lot 3 weeks ago. She is cooperative but appears anxious, glancing around quickly when a loud noise is heard outside the office. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. She takes levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and uses an over-the-counter inhaler as needed for exercise-induced asthma. Leukocyte count is 12,000/mm3 , and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 5.0 μU/mL. Examination shows dry skin and hair.

She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m2 . Rest and analgesics usually eradicate the pain within 2 weeks. She takes no medications except for an oral contraceptive. Medical history is remarkable for gestational diabetes mellitus during her pregnancies. She walks 3 miles daily for exercise and works as a sales representative for a computer software company. However, the pain seems to recur every 2 to 3 months. Vital signs are normal, and physical examination discloses no abnormalities.

She requests a laxative to help with her constipation. A 15-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of abdominal pain and constipation for the past several weeks. She is 158 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 43 kg (95 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2 .

He reports that he has had a 3-month history of fatigue, irritability, and feelings of hopelessness. A 37-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of inadequate control of his glucose concentrations for the past 2 months. He says that he has been noncompliant with his diabetic regimen, adding, "Sometimes I forget." Despite his poor control, he demands that he be discharged. He has been avoiding his family and friends because he is not in the mood to see them but admits that he is lonely. He did not get out of bed for 2 days, which prompted his wife to call an ambulance and have him admitted to the hospital. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. On mental status examination, he is tired and has a restricted affect. Prior to admission to the hospital, his only medication was insulin, although he often missed doses. There is no evidence of suicidal ideation. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. His fasting serum glucose concentration is 120 mg/dL. He is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 36 kg/m2 . He does not drink alcohol. Cognition is intact.

A 7-month-old infant, who was recently discharged from the hospital following an episode of enteritis and dehydration, has persistent watery diarrhea. His mother feeds him cow-milk formula and a variety of strained fruits and vegetables. No other abnormalities are seen. On physical examination, his temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), his mucous membranes are dry, and his abdomen is slightly distended.

The fetal head is engaged, the membranes are intact, the fetal heart tones are normal, and the cervix is 100% effaced and 7 cm dilated. A 25-year-old gravida 3 para 2 female is admitted to the hospital at 39 weeks' gestation in active labor. She had been having regular contractions every 4 minutes, but is now having only a few intermittent, weak contractions. Examination shows no reason for obstructed labor. She has received medication for pain twice in the past 6 hours.

She has not had previous episodes, although for more than 1 year she has had occasional difficulty passing stools. She is not in pain but is afraid to move her bowels for fear that the problem will worsen. She has no other symptoms. A 15-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because, she says, "something has been sticking out of my bottom since I had a bowel movement this morning." She has a 6-month-old child and lives with a 28-year-old female cousin. She has never been married and does not work or attend school. She tells you that she moved away from home more than a year ago and that her parents contribute nothing to her support.

Examination shows erythema, warmth, and induration of the upper back, buttocks, and posterior thighs. Her serum creatine kinase activity is 10,300 U/L. A 34-year-old white woman comes to the emergency department because of a persistent dull headache for the past 3 days. Examination of the head shows no abnormalities. Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; there is mild photophobia. Vital signs are temperature 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse 86/min, respirations 19/min, and blood pressure 182/100 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows striae, but is otherwise noncontributory. A serous effusion is noted on examination of the left tympanic membrane. A midsystolic click is heard best at the left sternal border; there are no murmurs or gallops. Mild expiratory wheezes are heard on auscultation of the chest.

She has begun smoking cigarettes, disobeying her curfew, and being truant from school. A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician after her mother learned that she began having sexual intercourse with various partners 1 month ago. Since the separation, however, she has become sullen, defiant, and rebellious. She does not use condoms or other contraception. The patient's parents separated 3 months ago. She had been an honor student and excelled in sports and leadership positions at school before the separation. The mother is concerned about her behavior.

A previously healthy 27-year-old man comes to the physician 4 weeks after noticing three nontender lesions on his penis. Examination shows three sessile, flesh-colored lesions on the shaft of the penis that are 10 mm in diameter. On application of a dilute solution of acetic acid, the lesions turn white. He takes no medications. He drinks two to five beers on social occasions. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F). He occasionally smokes marijuana. He says they have not changed in size. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. There is no lymphadenopathy. He is sexually active with multiple male and female partners and uses condoms inconsistently.

A 59-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 70/47 mm Hg. His oxyhemoglobin saturation in a central vein is 60% (N=70–75). Physical examination shows delayed capillary refill of the lips and nail beds and cool extremities. He also has been confused and agitated during this period. His current medication is a diuretic. He has a history of mild hypertension.
A 13-month-old child is brought to the emergency department because of urticaria, swelling of the lips, and difficulty breathing immediately after eating an egg.

Following the administration of desmopressin, urine osmolality increases. A 27-year-old man is admitted to the hospital 45 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. Laboratory studies show a serum glucose concentration within the reference range, increased serum osmolality, and decreased urine osmolality. Physical examination shows a sluggish response to stimuli. Two weeks later, the patient develops polyuria and polydipsia. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. A skull x-ray shows a linear, nondepressed basal skull fracture.

A 35-year-old female develops nausea and vomiting after she underwent a cholecystectomy for protracted ileus. The patient remains unable to eat 6 days after surgery. Her body mass index was 23 kg/m2 before surgery, and, except for the cholecystitis, she was in good health.

Intravenous glucose is administered, and the patient's symptoms improve. Her serum glucose concentration is 30 mg/dL. A 27-year-old nurse comes to the emergency department because of nervousness, dizziness, palpitations, and excess perspiration for the past 3 hours. She has had similar episodes over the past 6 months. Examination shows no abnormalities. The symptoms improve following ingestion of orange juice or soft drinks. She has been drinking two alcoholic beverages daily for the past month; before this time, she seldom drank alcohol. She says that she has had a great deal of stress.

Each episode of pain lasts for 1 second or less. The patient cannot tolerate touch over the right side of the face. CT scan of the head with and without contrast shows no abnormalities. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2 . Vital signs are normal. Medical history is remarkable for tension headaches, obesity, and gastric bypass surgery. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. The pain is often triggered by cold air, chewing, tactile stimulation, and brushing her teeth. She has had no trauma to the face or head. There is no facial weakness or loss of sensation. A 54-year-old woman comes to the office because she has had intermittent shooting pain over her right cheek and jaw during the past 3 weeks.

Measurement of hemoglobin A1c obtained last week was 5.4%. His diabetic diary shows home fingerstick blood glucose concentrations ranging from 140–200 mg/dL during the past 3 months. A 12-year-old boy with sickle cell disease and type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the office by his mother for an initial visit. His insulin regimen has not changed during the past year; however, his mother says he has been only marginally compliant with his insulin and dietary regimens. The patient's vital signs are temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse 72/min, respirations 24/min, and blood pressure 110/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. He admits to checking his glucose concentrations infrequently. Since that time, he has been treated with insulin and dietary management. Type 1 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed in the patient 6 years ago. The family recently moved to the area.

She presents to the office today to ask for help in dealing with midthoracic back pain to enable her to use less analgesic agents.

A 4-week-old male infant presented to the pediatric ophthalmology clinic with bilateral congenital corneal opacities. The white-to-white corneal diameters were 10 mm horizontally and vertically in both eyes, and B-scan ultrasonography revealed unremarkable posterior segments. His corneal abnormalities were noted by the neonatologists on the first day of life. . Examination under anesthesia revealed bilateral corneal opacities with peripheral clearing and absent red reflexes. The pregnancy was full-term and uncomplicated, and he was delivered spontaneously without the use of forceps. A systemic survey revealed no other dysmorphic findings. He was referred to the clinic for further evaluation and management.

A 55-year-old woman with small cell carcinoma of the lung is admitted to the hospital to undergo chemotherapy. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Six days after treatment is started, she develops a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F). Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 100/mm3 (5% segmented neutrophils and 95% lymphocytes).

Examination shows a migrating serpiginous pruritic perianal rash. Her leukocyte count is 8000/mm3 with 20% eosinophils. A 14-year-old girl has had nausea, intermittent diarrhea, and a 2.2-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 4 weeks.

The patient is using insurance coverage through his wife but does not wish for his diagnosis to be disclosed to anyone. He is on probation after a conviction for aggravated robbery 3 years ago. There is also a warrant for his arrest for assault and battery. He says he has tried repeatedly to abstain from cocaine use but lives in a part of town where there are heavy drug sales. A 37-year-old Anglo-American man is admitted to the hospital for treatment for cocaine dependency. He did not like his hospital outpatient group but liked his single session at Cocaine Anonymous. Physical examination shows a thin man with good muscle strength and no focal neurologic deficits. Vital signs are temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 70/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 125/85 mm Hg.

A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a physical examination prior to participating in sports. He is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Serum concentrations of gonadotropic hormones, estrogens, and testosterone are within the reference ranges. Pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. Physical examination shows bilateral 1.5-cm fibroglandular masses located beneath the nipple-areolar complex and normal penis and testes. He appears reluctant to remove his shirt for the examination, and says that he is embarrassed because he has grown breasts during the past year.

Examination of the back shows bilateral paravertebral muscle spasm. A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of nonradiating low back pain for 3 days. The pain began after he worked in his yard. Vital signs are within normal limits. Range of motion is limited by pain. He has not had any change in bowel movements or urination. Straight-leg raising is negative. He had one similar episode 3 years ago that resolved spontaneously.

Her last menstrual period ended 6 days ago. She is sexually active and does not use any contraception. A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because she has had increasingly severe lower abdominal pain and nausea for the past 2 days. Temperature is 38.3°C (101.0°F). Pelvic examination discloses leukorrhea at the cervical os and tenderness of the uterus to palpation. The adnexal areas are tender but no masses are palpable. Physical examination discloses abdominal tenderness in the lower quadrants bilaterally with rebound and guarding.

Physical examination discloses thickening and hardening of the skin over the dorsum of the hands and forearms, as well as mild kyphosis. During the interview, her face is expressionless. The patient does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages. She has a flexed posture and is unable to open her mouth wide. Vital signs are normal. She is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 81 kg (179 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2 . Family history is significant for stable angina in her father and rheumatoid arthritis in her mother. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable and the patient takes no medications. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Passive and active range of motion of the upper extremities is full. Strength testing shows no abnormalities; muscle tension is normal. A 57-year-old woman comes to the office for a preoperative evaluation 2 weeks before undergoing scheduled laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Gait is slow and deliberate. The patient has a 102-year-old grandmother who resides in a nursing care facility and has Parkinson disease.

Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland confirms a solid, 1-cm nodule. Medical history is unremarkable and he takes no routine medications. The patient has been generally healthy. Vital signs are normal. A 40-year-old man comes to the office for a preemployment physical examination.
A 2-month-old female is brought to the office for her first routine health maintenance examination and for her immunization update.

Physical examination discloses mild subcostal and intercostal retractions.

Results show that the new drug is significantly better than standard treatment. A total of 1000 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are enrolled. The alpha and beta values for calculating probability are 0.05 and 0.20, respectively.

He denies any trauma but reports that he had been doing a lot of painting over the past week. He denies any radicular pain or numbness. He rates the pain as a 7 on a scale of 0 to 10 scale. Four hours later the physician receives a call from the local emergency department, where the patient presented confused, nauseated, and vertiginous.

The pain is usually relieved with defecation and does not occur at night or interfere with sleep. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. She says she is frustrated by her symptoms and has stopped traveling because of her frequent, urgent need to use the bathroom.
