An intravenous catheter is placed. Fetal heart rate is 144/min. Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Vital signs are temperature 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse 132/min, respirations 32/min, and blood pressure 135/78 mm Hg. A grade 3/6, low-pitched, diastolic, rumbling murmur is audible at the apex; a distinct snapping sound precedes the murmur.

A 47-year-old man comes to the physician 12 hours after the sudden onset of a severe occipital headache and stiff neck. His temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. He has hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He is oriented to person, place, and time. He has not had any other symptoms and has no history of severe headache. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Range of motion of the neck is decreased due to pain. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide and ranitidine.

Molecular testing for FBN1 shows a single nucleotide difference that does not change the amino acid at that locus. She is at the 95th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. The same nucleotide change is found in 15 of 200 individuals without Marfan syndrome. Her mother is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall. A 10-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because her school nurse thinks that she may have Marfan syndrome. There is no clinical evidence of Marfan syndrome in the mother, but she has the same single nucleotide change as the patient. Physical examination shows a narrow palate with dental crowding, long slender extremities, and joint laxity.

She gives dramatic and exaggerated descriptions of her present and past symptoms, and she makes conflicting statements about her history. Review of her extensive medical chart, which she has brought with her, discloses that she has a long history of varying physical symptoms. She has been hospitalized at least 23 times since age 18 years. A 50-year-old woman comes to the office for the first time because of recurrent abdominal pain. Definitive causes for these symptoms have not been found despite extensive diagnostic studies, consultations with many physicians, and several surgical explorations.

A 5-year-old boy returns to the office with his 19-year-old mother to discuss results of studies done to evaluate his behavior of eating dirt. Height, weight, and BMI are at the 50th percentile. I try to stop him from eating dirt, but I'm not around much since I work two jobs." She says he has a good appetite but has had a habit of eating sand and dirt since age 3 years. She says, "I don't know where he gets that habit. I used to eat dirt, but I stopped years ago. Serologic testing confirms toxoplasmosis. He has not had fever, sweats, or chills. The patient sits quietly while his mother answers questions about his health. He has said his head hurts three or four times during the past 2 weeks. The patient takes no medications. Vital signs are normal. Vaccinations are upto-date. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities except for symmetrical nontender cervical adenopathy. Results of laboratory studies, including serum zinc, lead, and iron concentrations, are within the reference ranges. She says her son seems healthy, although he does not seem to be as active as other children his age.

No sperm are seen on semen analysis. He has mild gynecomastia and small, firm testicles. A 32-year-old man and his 29-year-old wife come to the office for evaluation for infertility. The husband is 188 cm (6 ft 3 in) tall with fair skin and little facial hair. The wife's gynecologist has reported that her anatomic and physiologic evaluation disclosed no abnormalities and that assessment of potential male factors is needed.

The patient is interested in using a nicotine patch and bupropion therapy because he says his friend found the treatments to be helpful. A 28-year-old man comes to the office because he would like to quit smoking cigarettes. He does not drink alcoholic beverages or use illicit drugs. He takes no medications. Medical history is remarkable for childhood febrile seizures. I even wake up at night to smoke." Vital signs are normal. The patient began smoking cigarettes at age 12 years; he was smoking two packs of cigarettes daily by age 17 years, and he has not curtailed his use since that time. He says, "I cannot go more than a day without cigarettes because I get so anxious and irritable.

A 40-year-old male presents to the office with symptoms of odynophagia and gastroesophageal reflux. Rectal examination demonstrates brown stool that is positive for occult blood. The patient's tilt test result and hemoglobin level are normal. Past medical history reveals AIDS, and his most recent CD4 count was 30 cells/mcL. He also says that he experienced hematemesis once last week.

Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. A 53-year-old woman with a history of stage IVA1 (T4N1M0B2) mycosis fungoides presented with a new 1-month history of hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa (Figure 1). Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Other notable findings on examination were 1- to 2-cm lymphadenopathy in the bilateral inguinal folds and axillae. The patient had previously received 5 cycles of romidepsin with progression of disease, followed by 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin hydrochloride, which was followed by partial response.Black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. . Review of systems was notable for fatigue.

A 32-year-old woman who was admitted to the hospital for fever, flulike symptoms, and altered mental status developed sudden-onset blurry vision in her right eye. Her history was notable for phthisis in her left eye due to a left orbit clear cell sarcoma with metastatic disease, after surgical excision and radiation, with recent enrollment in a palliative immunotherapy research protocol. One day later, her mental status improved, and she reported central blurry vision in her right eye. After completing 2 days of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and antivirals for presumed septic meningitis, her laboratory and imaging results returned negative and she was transitioned to intravenous methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg). On examination, her visual acuity was 20/40 in this eye, she had normal intraocular pressure, and there was no evidence of anterior chamber or vitreous cells. Dilated fundus examination revealed segmental areas of venous sheathing (Figure 1A) in the right eye and was not possible in the left eye owing to phthisis. An optical coherence tomography scan of the right eye revealed hyperreflective changes along the outer plexiform and outer nuclear layers, small intraretinal cysts, and disruption of the ellipsoid and especially the interdigitation zone (Figure 1B).A, Color fundus photograph of the right eye at the time of presentation demonstrating segmental areas of venous sheathing (white arrowheads). B, Optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrating hyperreflective changes in the outer plexiform and outer nuclear layers (blue bracket), small intraretinal cystic spaces (red arrowheads), and disruption of the ellipsoid and especially the interdigitation zone (yellow arrowheads) corresponding to the dark areas on near infrared (white arrowheads).Obtain information about the immunotherapy protocol initiated for her sarcoma.

Physical examination revealed multiple 1-mm flesh-colored follicular papules and keratin spines against a diffuse erythematous background affecting the face (Figure, A and B) and upper trunk. Results of skin biopsy from the right ear demonstrated dilatation and keratotic plugging of the hair infundibula with marked dystrophy and expansion of the inner root sheath. Immunohistochemical analysis for SV40 polyomavirus was positive (Figure, D).Photographs of (A) forehead and (B) nose depicting multiple follicular papules and keratin spines against a diffuse erythematous background. The inner root sheath cells were enlarged with irregular trichohyaline granules and apoptotic cells with abrupt cornification without formation of a granular layer (Figure, C). Subsequently it spread to involve nose, chin, upper trunk, and extremities. Her scalp and eyebrow hairs were unremarkable. A woman in her 70s presented with a 1-year history of a facial cutaneous eruption initially affecting malar cheeks and eyebrows. Her medical history included a cadaveric renal transplant 2 years earlier for end-stage renal failure. Immunosuppressant medications included mycophenolate mofetil, 200 mg, twice daily and tacrolimus, 8 mg, twice daily. The lesions were mildly pruritic. D, SV40 polyomavirus stain (original magnification ×40). Serology results were unremarkable. C, Hematoxylin-eosin staining (original magnification ×40). . Tacrolimus levels were therapeutic.

Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. His pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 165/95 mm Hg. He is currently taking no medications. A 55-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine physical examination.

The patient recalls that at one point during the operation he experienced a sudden, intense feeling of overwhelming fear. A 54-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 10 days after undergoing a stereotactic brain operation to remove a small tumor. During the procedure, he was under conscious sedation. The operation was successful.

Examination shows a tender, erythematous, edematous left ankle; there is point tenderness over the medial malleolus. A bone scan shows increased uptake in the left lower tibial metaphysis. Two years ago, a culture from an abscess in the cervical region grew Staphylococcus aureus. A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of fever and painful swelling of the left ankle. Culture of bone aspirate grows Serratia marcescens. He has had recurrent cervical lymphadenitis and pneumonia since infancy. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Nitroblue tetrazolium test shows no color change.

A total of 5000 patients with essential hypertension are enrolled and randomly assigned to one of two groups: 2500 patients receive the new drug and 2500 patients receive placebo. A placebo-controlled clinical trial is conducted to assess whether a new antihypertensive drug is more effective than standard therapy.

A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-day history of fever, severe muscle pain, and diffuse, painful swelling of his neck, underarms, and groin area. Examination of the right upper extremity shows an erythematous, solid, tender mass on the underside of the upper extremity just above the elbow; the mass is draining blood and necrotic material. The symptoms began after returning from a camping trip in New Mexico. Physical examination shows generalized scattered black maculae. He appears ill and lethargic and can barely answer questions. His temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg.

A 26-year-old woman with HIV infection comes to the office because of a 4-day history of pain and redness of her left lower leg. Current medications include antiretroviral therapy and ibuprofen as needed. There is a 5×8-cm area on the anterior surface of her left lower extremity that is swollen, erythematous, and tender. She previously has developed a rash after taking erythromycin, and she has had an anaphylactic response to penicillin. Vital signs are temperature 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse 86/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 138/70 mm Hg. She says the symptoms began after she tripped over a tree branch in her yard and scraped her left leg.

During episodes, she experiences the acute onset of rotatory vertigo and imbalance, decreased hearing, tinnitus, a sense of fullness of the right ear, and vomiting. Examination shows a mild hearing loss of the right ear. A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of two 12-hour episodes of dizziness over the past 3 months.

A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of sore throat and fever. There is a white exudate on the right tonsil. Examination of the oropharynx shows erythema, edema, and anterior displacement of the right side of the soft palate. The uvula is deviated to the left. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. She has been taking acetaminophen since her symptoms began. Medical history is unremarkable and she takes no routine medications. During the past 3 days, she also has noticed a change in her voice and has had increased pain with swallowing. Vital signs are temperature 40.0°C (104.0°F), pulse 130/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 102/66 mm Hg. Palpation of the neck discloses enlarged, tender, mobile anterior cervical lymph nodes. Trismus is noted.

Paroxysmal episodes of headache, sweating, anxiety, nausea, and vomiting occur frequently. A CT scan reveals a left adrenal mass. A 45-year-old female presents to the office for evaluation of unexplained elevations of her blood pressure.

A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision. Sensation to pinprick is absent over the right side of the face anterior to the right ear, extending down along the full extent of the mandible to the chin. Sensation also is absent over the right side of the tongue. He is conscious. The gag reflex is present. Physical examination shows numerous lacerations and ecchymoses over the face. His vision is normal. Ocular, facial, and lingual movements are intact. He was the unrestrained driver. X-rays of the skull show fractures of the orbit, zygomatic arch, and infratemporal fossa.

A 59-year-old black woman with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes presented with a 2-month history of a rapidly enlarging tender nodule on her right fifth digit. Physical examination showed a single 25-mm, firm, dome-shaped subcutaneous nodule with central ulceration on the lateral aspect of the right fifth digit (Figure 1). No lymphadenopathy was present.Dome-shaped subcutaneous nodule with central ulceration on the lateral aspect of the right fifth digit. She denied fevers, joint pain, joint stiffness, inciting trauma, or recent outdoor activity. There was no erythema, edema, fluctuance, induration, or lymphangitis surrounding the lesion. Results of a recent complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic profile were unremarkable. She had no history of immunosuppression. .

A 3-week-old male infant is brought to the office by his mother because of a 2-day history of white lesions in the mouth. The infant was born at term via uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery; he has been breast-feeding well and is urinating and having bowel movements normally. Physical examination discloses white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that do not come off when gently scraped with a tongue blade. Today, he weighs 3629 kg (8 lb; 25th percentile). Vital signs are normal. He appears adequately hydrated. At birth, he weighed 3289 g (7 lb 4 oz; 30th percentile).

A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of right shoulder pain that began after he chopped wood 2 days ago. The pain is reproduced when the patient is asked to externally rotate the shoulder against resistance; there is no weakness. Examination of the right upper extremity shows no obvious bone deformities or point tenderness.

A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of easy bruising for 4 months. Her hemoglobin concentration is 13 g/dL, leukocyte count is 5000/mm3 , and platelet count is 35,000/mm3 . She has a history of lung cancer treated with radiation therapy 6 months ago. She has a 2-year history of hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic and an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. A serum antiplatelet antibody assay is negative. Examination, including neurologic examination, shows no abnormalities except for multiple ecchymoses.

A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because she is concerned that she may have contracted meningitis from her soccer teammate, who was diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis and admitted to the hospital yesterday. The patient's soccer team traveled to a neighboring state to participate in a tournament 1 week ago and she shared a hotel room with the girl who was hospitalized. Medical history is remarkable for asthma. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Medications include inhaled albuterol. Vital signs are temperature 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse 64/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 107/58 mm Hg. The patient feels well but is concerned she may have "caught the same bug."

Physical examination discloses a systolic heart murmur over the precordium. A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because, she says, "I'm burning up." Medical history is significant for intravenous drug use.

A 26-year-old male police officer comes to the office for an annual health maintenance examination. He is physically active and feels well, but he notes that his asthma has been more active during the past month. He says that he has had to use his albuterol inhaler one to two times daily for wheezing and chest tightness. He has had coldand exercise-induced asthma for the past 14 years. He is 188 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 90 kg (200 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2 . Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for scattered rhonchi and wheezes with forced expiration. Vital signs are temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 70/min, respirations 12/min, and blood pressure 120/76 mm Hg. He has not had gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, productive cough, or fever. He takes no other medications. Medical history is remarkable for atopic allergies, especially to pollen and cats. Peak expiratory flow rate is 240 L/min.

A previously healthy 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department in August 1 hour after the onset of headache, dizziness, nausea, and one episode of vomiting. His symptoms began during the first hour of full-contact football practice in full uniform. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 90/65 mm Hg. He is not oriented to person, place, or time. On arrival, he is diaphoretic. He reported feeling weak and faint but did not lose consciousness. He vomited once after drinking water. Examination, including neurologic examination, shows no other abnormalities.
A new severe respiratory illness caused by a newly identified virus is discovered.

This morning he soaked his thigh in a tub of hot water and massaged it, after which a large amount of "greenish fluid" drained from the wound sites. Palpation of the burn sites discloses fluctuance. A 43-year-old man with a history of self-mutilation comes to the emergency department because of pain in his right thigh and shaking chills during the past 3 days. Physical examination shows an edematous right lateral thigh with multiple burn sites with a white exudative appearance. He says he intentionally burned his right thigh several times with a cigarette lighter 6 days ago. Vital signs are temperature 39.2°C (102.5°F), pulse 170/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg. The patient normally takes lithium carbonate but stopped 3 months ago after he lost his job. Results of laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 14 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 19,000/mm3 . There is erythema surrounding the burn areas with red streaks extending up the thigh. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable.

He states that he is delighted with his newfound energy and reports that he now needs only 4 hours of sleep nightly. He has a labile affect. He has a history of drinking alcohol excessively and using methamphetamines and cocaine during his 20s, but he has not consumed alcohol or used illicit drugs for the past 3 years. He has had no delusions or hallucinations. He frequently stops working on his own tasks to attempt to develop greater efficiency in his shop. His speech is rapid in rate but normal in rhythm, and his thought process is organized. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 60/min, and blood pressure is 125/80 mm Hg. Short- and long-term memory are intact. Attention and concentration are fair; he makes no errors when performing serial sevens, and he can repeat seven digits forward and five in reverse sequence. He works as an automobile mechanic. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. He has no history of psychiatric illness. He always performed well in school. On mental status examination, he describes his mood as "good." A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because he has had difficulty focusing on tasks at work and at home during the past 2 months. He has had a lot of energy for work but often is distracted to the point that he does not complete assigned tasks.

A computed tomography scan with multiplanar reconstruction was also performed (Figure 1B).A, A plain abdominal x-ray shows a huge colonic distension and a clear coffee-bean-like or “bent inner tube” sign is visible. At physical examination the patient was pale, sweaty, peripherally hypoperfused, tachypnoeic, and dehydrated, and the abdomen was extremely distended, diffusely tympanic, and tender at palpation. A 77-year-old institutionalized and bedridden man with severe Alzheimer dementia and long-standing schizophrenia was admitted to the emergency department for bowel obstruction with progressive abdominal distension and tenderness. A plain abdominal radiograph showed a huge colonic distension (Figure 1A). B, A computed tomography scan with multiplanar reconstruction. His blood pressure was 90/70 mm Hg, his heart rate was 114 beats per minute, his oxygen saturation was at 90%, his arterial blood gas pH level was 7.43, his partial pressure of carbon dioxide was 32, his partial pressure of oxygen 68, his laceration lactate level was 5.0, and his white blood cell count was 24 000 mm3. His family members and caregivers accompanied him. .

A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm and a soft S3. Pulmonary examination shows crackles at both lung bases. There is 2+ pitting edema of the lower legs and ankles. Jugular venous pressure is 15 cm H2O. A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of painless swelling of both ankles. Her pulse is 96/min and regular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. She has been awakened from sleep by shortness of breath. She also reports shortness of breath with exertion and when lying down. She has not had chest pain.

Examination of the right upper extremity shows erythema and moderate edema. A 32-year-old man who is a jackhammer operator comes to the physician because of pain and swelling of his right arm for 3 days. Capillary refill time is less than 3 seconds. The symptoms are moderately exacerbated by exertion.

A 63-year-old woman is in the hospital recovery room 4 hours after elective left hemicolectomy for colon carcinoma at the splenic flexure. Vital signs now are temperature 35.8°C (96.4°F), pulse 130/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg. The nurse tells you the patient's blood pressure has progressively declined since the operation. Hematocrit is 30%; preoperative hematocrit was 41%. Medical history is significant for hypertension and coronary artery disease. The patient has received 4 L of intravenous crystalloid in the recovery room. Drainage from the nasogastric tube is clear. Reported operative blood loss was 200 mL. Physical examination discloses a slightly distended abdomen with an intact incision. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Urine output has been 10 mL during the past 2 hours. She has a preoperative written directive for no blood products through transfusion for religious reasons.

Genetic testing for the 36 most common mutations shows a detectable mutation (G551D) in one allele of the CFTR gene. She says that her sweat is salty and crystallizes on her skin. A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of abdominal pain. She has a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, and pancreatitis. She has thick nasal secretions. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness. Her vital signs are within normal limits.

His sister states that he recently saw a psychiatrist for the first time because of hearing voices; he was prescribed a medication, but she is not sure what it is. Examination shows profuse diaphoresis and muscle rigidity. The abdomen is soft and nontender. His leukocyte count is 15,600/mm3 , and serum creatine kinase activity is 943 U/L. He is unable to answer questions. He appears acutely ill. His temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F), pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 160/102 mm Hg. Mental status examination shows psychomotor agitation alternating with lethargy. His neck is supple. A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his sister because of increasing confusion for 10 hours. She says that he has a history of excessive drinking, and she thinks that he has also experimented with illicit drugs.

A 16-year-old boy is admitted to the emergency department because of a knife wound to the left side of his chest. An x-ray of the chest shows an air-fluid level in the left side of the chest, partial collapse of the left lung, and elevation of the stomach bubble. The mediastinum is in the midline.

Medical history is remarkable for coronary artery disease, for which he takes atorvastatin, furosemide, carvedilol, lisinopril, and 81-mg aspirin. A 72-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit for pain management and observation of ventricular ectopy 4 hours after undergoing uncomplicated left total knee replacement. He is receiving fentanyl via systemic patient-controlled analgesic pump for pain management. Vital signs now are temperature 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Physical examination discloses no unexpected abnormalities. Baseline echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 0.20.

A 67-year-old woman has had fatigue, dry skin, brittle hair, swelling of the ankles, and cold intolerance for 1 year; she has gained 9 kg (20 lb) during this period. The relaxation phase of the Achilles reflex is greatly prolonged. She appears lethargic. There is mild edema of the ankles bilaterally. Examination shows dry skin and a nontender thyroid gland that is enlarged to two times its normal size. Her pulse is 55/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg.

She refuses to cooperate in contacting the father, who could be a translocation carrier. At today's visit, she reacts angrily when the issue of contacting the child's father for testing is raised. The relationship between the parents is hostile. She states that he abandoned them and that he has no interest in his child. A 2-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for follow-up of a chromosome analysis done 1 month ago. Chromosome analysis showed a small unbalanced chromosome translocation, with extra chromosomal material at the tip of chromosome 3. You do not know the father, but an office worker told you that he lives in a nearby town. The child has minor dysmorphic features, and growth and developmental delay. The mother says that he is living with a new girlfriend. The cytogenetics laboratory requested blood samples from both parents for follow-up studies. The parents are divorced, and the mother has custody of the child. The mother has been tested and has normal chromosomes without evidence of translocation.

A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever and left ear pain for 3 days. There is edema and tenderness behind the left ear. She has been treated with amoxicillin for the past 5 days for left otitis media. Examination shows the left ear displaced forward and laterally from the head. Otoscopic examination shows a red, dull, left tympanic membrane that does not move. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg.

A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram was performed, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit, and a transesophageal echocardiogram was obtained (Figure 1).Transesophageal echocardiogram obtained from the patient in diastole on the midesophageal long-axis view. A 61-year-old man with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of fever, dyspnea, and generalized weakness. A soft S1 was present on cardiac examination, and crackles were auscultated in basilar lung fields bilaterally. He was diaphoretic and had poor dentition. His vital signs were temperature, 38.4°C (101.1°F); blood pressure, 94/40 mm Hg; heart rate, 116/min; and respiratory rate, 26/min. Three sets of blood cultures from different sites were obtained. Cardiology, cardiac surgery, and infectious disease physicians were consulted. .

X-rays of the spine show a compression fracture of L1-2. A bisphosphonate drug is prescribed. A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of low back pain for 1 week. A DEXA scan shows decreased bone mineral density. Physical examination shows localized tenderness over the lumbar spine after movement. Serum calcium and phosphorus concentrations and serum alkaline phosphatase activity are within the reference ranges. Menopause occurred 10 years ago.

A 72-year-old woman who has smoked 20 cigarettes daily for the past 38 years begins using eyedrops for glaucoma. Three days later, she has a marked increase in shortness of breath while walking up a flight of stairs.

The patient refuses lumbar puncture for examination of cerebrospinal fluid. Complete blood count shows a leukocyte count of 18,000/mm3 with 23% band neutrophils. A 38-year-old man with Down syndrome and severe mental retardation is brought to the emergency department by ambulance because of increasing lethargy for the past several hours. The patient's caregiver, who is also the patient's guardian, cannot be located and staff at the group home where the patient resides cannot be reached by telephone. Auscultation of the chest discloses clear lungs; cardiac examination discloses a systolic click. On physical examination the patient is awake but lethargic. Toxicologic screening of the urine is negative. Serum electrolyte concentrations are normal. Neurologic examination shows decreased muscle tone. Vital signs are temperature 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 19/min, and blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg. The patient is noncommunicative and you are unable to obtain an initial history of his present illness or a past medical history. You do not know if he takes any medications.

She says that she needs the morphine to treat her pain, but she is worried that she is becoming addicted. She is receiving intravenous morphine via a patient-controlled pump. She drinks one to two glasses of wine weekly. She has no history of substance use disorder. During the operation, plastic reconstruction of facial fractures, and open reduction and internal fixation of the left femur are also done. Thirty-six hours postoperatively, she is awake but not completely alert. After being severely beaten and sustaining a gunshot wound to the abdomen, a 42-year-old woman undergoes resection of a perforated small bowel.

Chvostek and Trousseau signs are present. His serum calcium concentration is 6.5 mg/dL. A 57-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of cramping in his hands and feet and numbness and tingling around his lips and in his fingers; these symptoms occurred intermittently for 6 months but have been progressively severe during the past 2 weeks. The abdomen is nontender. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally. His pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 105/65 mm Hg. He has a 10-year history of drinking 8 to 10 beers daily. He also has had a 13-kg (30-lb) weight loss and bulky, foul-smelling stools that do not flush easily. He appears cachectic and chronically ill. He has been hospitalized twice for severe abdominal pain 4 and 6 years ago.

She and her husband live on a farm 90 miles from the nearest dialysis facility. A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for replacement of her left knee joint due to degenerative joint disease. Reversible causes of renal failure have been excluded. She is a retired seamstress. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus, a long history of hypertension, and chronic renal failure presumed secondary to diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Serum creatinine concentration on admission was 6.0 mg/dL. Her current therapy includes a low-sodium, low-protein American Diabetes Association (ADA) diet, enalapril, and acetaminophen. She underwent a tonsillectomy at age 9 years and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 68 years.

Routine laboratory studies reveal a leukocyte count of 25.0 × 103/mcL (reference range 4.5-11.0 × 103/mcL) and 97% mature-appearing lymphocytes on a peripheral blood smear. A 75-year-old female presents to the office for a health maintenance examination. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrate the lymphocytes to be of B-cell origin. She says that she is more fatigued than she was at 65, but she still gardens and drives to the grocery store.

Pelvic examination shows a 4 x 3-cm, tender, fluctuant mass medial to the left labium majus compromising the introital opening. A previously healthy 27-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of moderate-to-severe pain and swelling of the left labia. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 115/75 mm Hg. She is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently.

A previously healthy 24-year-old woman who is a college student comes to the office because of a 6-month history of abdominal bloating, upper abdominal discomfort, and constipation. The symptoms are more severe when she is preparing for examinations but improve after bowel movements. She takes no medications. A urease breath test result is negative. Her pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 100/72 mm Hg. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2 . Physical examination, including digital rectal examination, shows no other abnormalities. She does not smoke or use illicit drugs. A man in his late 60s with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes for more than 10 years that was complicated by neuropathy and retinopathy presented with persistent chorea in the left upper extremity for about 1 month despite aggressive correction with insulin. His home medications were carefully reviewed to rule out any medications that could cause chorea. The patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure), which showed a T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion.
